title: R29 Plugin Scheduling Requirements History

versions.body:
# R29 Plugin Scheduling Requirements History

The initial note raised an ordering question: when user-provided custom plugins and external CCM both enter addon processing in R29, how should the resource tasks be ordered? Here, "both" only means they were mentioned together in the same round of release discussions, not that they had been confirmed to share a task node.

The starting point for tracing this back is `pkg/addons/ensure.go`. The file belongs to the `addons` package; the earlier investigation followed the issue name and call names to the area around this entry point. This location is enough to guide further investigation of where user plugins connect, but the directory and package names alone cannot establish task order or whether external CCM initialization has already occurred on the same branch.

The first draft listed three arrangements:

- Handle external CCM first, then consider user plugins;
- Insert user plugins after the embedded plugins finish;
- Create a user plugin task regardless of the configuration contents, and let the task itself decide whether there is anything to do.

The third option was set aside first. Without Addons configuration, the task has no clear target; even if it can return quietly during execution, a node would still remain in the graph. People reading the task graph later would conflate "no plugin work" with "a skipped piece of work." This was a concern about the meaning of the task graph; there were no configuration samples or scenario results at the time.

There was also insufficient justification for putting external CCM first. It only reflected an intuition that external components should seemingly be prepared first, without explaining why user plugins must wait or whether the user plugin branch should still appear when configuration is missing. This version therefore does not record external CCM first as the default arrangement.

The review required separating two questions: first, why the user plugin task appears; then, where an existing task should be placed. The two questions cannot both be answered with "enters the addon flow." Reaching the processing entry point does not mean a user plugin task has been created.

Another item raised alongside this was the missing Kubernetes 1.29 e2e scenario. The only note here is to check the platform and version combination in the build configuration. A scenario that completes cluster creation shows, at most, that the path reached a result state; it cannot substitute for assessing the edges of the user plugin task.

Tentative decision: do not adopt unconditional creation of the user plugin task; do not treat external CCM first as the default position. Continue tracing back from the task hookup to find the actual connection point between user plugins and external CCM.

versions.body:
# Evolution of R29 Plugin Scheduling Requirements

The original records from 2023 lumped user plugins and external CCM together under the phrase "addon processing". Written this way, the debate seemed to be only about ordering; looking back revealed a more fundamental question that came before ordering: whether user plugins qualified as resource tasks in the first place. With these two judgments mixed together, the position of external CCM could easily be used as a substitute for configuration conditions.

`pkg/addons/ensure.go` remains the starting point for the review. The file declares that it belongs to the `addons` package, and the earlier investigation arrived here via issue names and call names. This entry point indicates that the area around user plugin integration is worth inspecting, but the resource task graph cannot be inferred from the path name, nor can the file's directory be treated as the execution location of external CCM. The original records retained only navigation around the entry point, not a complete task graph, configuration structure, or sample runs.

## Three Arrangements Retained in the Original Draft

Three arrangements were compared at the time. The first had external CCM processed first, on the grounds that external components appeared to need preparation in advance. The second placed user plugins after embedded plugins, on the grounds that user-provided content was closer to plugin resources. The third always created a user plugin task and then let the task decide internally whether to return, on the grounds that this removed a branch from graph construction.

The third arrangement was not approved. Without Addons configuration, the task has nothing to process; even if it can return silently during execution, the task node has already conflated "no plugin work" with "a piece of work that was skipped". The review concluded that this distinction should be preserved during graph construction rather than hidden inside the task. This judgment concerns only the conditions under which a user plugin task appears, and does not attempt to define other initialization conditions for external CCM.

At this point, "no configuration" and "configuration exists but is not enabled" still cannot be described as the same situation. The original records did not retain the corresponding fields, default values, or configuration samples. Combining them into "empty configuration" saves words, but obscures the conditions that actually need to be confirmed later. Such shorthand in the old draft is therefore retained as wording used at the time, not as a judgment to continue citing.

The first arrangement did not become a decision either. Running external CCM first was only a conjecture based on convenience: it did not answer why user plugins should wait, or whether a user plugin task had already been created. If the ordering cannot explain why a task appears, ordering cannot be treated as the only issue.

## Review Addendum

The review did not ask for the entire addon lifecycle to be redrawn, only for the order of verification to be stated clearly. The addendum proposed first confirming whether the Addons configuration object exists; then confirming whether it is enabled if it exists; next checking which phase user plugin operations enter; and finally checking where external CCM initialization continues from.

This sequence is not a flowchart covering all addons. It simply avoids inferring intermediate tasks from the final state. For example, the absence of obvious abnormalities after external CCM initialization does not prove that user plugins have run; likewise, a user plugin showing no changes in a particular run does not directly establish the position of external CCM. An intermediate node may never have been created, or it may have been created and then skipped; these two cases need to be examined separately.

The old notes contain the sentence: "As long as the addons flow is entered, there will be a user plugin task." This statement is now marked as no longer adopted. Entering processing and creating a task are not the same thing. Another old suggestion was to check the initialization result of external CCM first; if there were no abnormalities at the end, user plugin work would not need to be listed separately. This was intended to shorten the investigation path at the time, but was later crossed out as well: the final state cannot show whether user plugins were scheduled, skipped, or never entered the task graph at all.

The meeting side notes also retained a broader statement: external CCM is near addon processing, and ordering can be revisited after the scenarios are filled in. This statement explains why the discussion was not immediately closed at the time, but it did not become a decision. Scenario coverage and resource task edges are related issues, and neither should be used to draw conclusions about the other.

## Attempt to Combine the Review with Kubernetes 1.29 Scenarios

The "missing Kubernetes 1.29 e2e scenarios" came up during the same period. Someone proposed finding a version scenario that could complete cluster creation or an upgrade and observing the final addon state along the way, to eliminate one round of verification. This approach was not adopted as evidence of ordering.

A scenario can prove that a path reached its resulting state, but does not inherently show whether user plugins came before or after external CCM, or whether their tasks were never created. It also does not show whether an empty task appeared when there was no Addons configuration. Therefore, replacing task graph inspection with existing 1.29 scenarios would merge the two issues back into the original draft's vague wording.

The approach retained at the time was to review them separately: for task ordering, return to the resource task graph and the user plugin integration point; for missing scenarios, return to the platform and version combinations in the build configuration. Adding a scenario entry point does not mean that ordering has been confirmed, and verifying ordering does not mean that 1.29 coverage is complete.

A quick investigation plan is still preserved on the old page: first run the existing 1.29 scenarios, and if the final addon state shows no abnormalities, temporarily defer examining the relative positions of user plugins and CCM. This plan is now marked as abandoned. At the time, it could only narrow the scope of suspicion; it could not answer the conditions under which a task exists, nor explain task edges.

## Decisions Retained in This Round

The approach of creating a user plugin task without configuration is not adopted, nor is running external CCM first documented as the default arrangement. User plugins retain a candidate position after embedded plugins complete and before external CCM initialization, but this version does not present that candidate position as a confirmed public rule.

Three items still need to be reviewed: the conditions for creating the user plugin node; the task edges between that node and external CCM initialization; and which build configuration contains the missing Kubernetes 1.29 e2e scenarios. A single observation of the final state cannot substitute for the first two, and addon ordering notes cannot substitute for the last.

Addendum: If a scenario entry point is found later, it can initially be treated only as a clue to version coverage. Whether the run passed through the respective phases of user plugins and external CCM still needs to be confirmed against the resource task graph. This restriction is intended to avoid reinterpreting a successful cluster result as a conclusion about ordering.

# Evolution of R29 Plugin Scheduling Requirements

This record began as nothing more than a release closeout note. Custom plugins and external CCM were mentioned in the same round of discussion, and the question was phrased as "which gets handled first". Later, the missing Kubernetes 1.29 e2e scenarios were also placed alongside it. Old links led from the addon entry point all the way to the topic of scenarios, making it easy for readers to mistake a test entry point for evidence of ordering.

Looking back now, the two questions were indeed adjacent, but they were not the same decision: one concerned whether user plugins enter the resource task graph and their relative phase within that graph; the other concerned whether all platform and version combinations for the 1.29 scenarios were present in the build configuration. This page preserves the process by which the two were once mixed together in the text, as well as the reasons they were later separated. It is not a complete description of the addon lifecycle; the surviving material is only sufficient to explain why this user-plugin edge was finalized separately.

## The Earliest Recorded Entry-Point Assessment

The records from 2023 begin with `pkg/addons/ensure.go`. The only visible information about the file was that it belonged to the `addons` package and had an import section below the file header. The earlier investigation reached this location by following issue names and call names, so the early notes described it as "near the user-plugin integration point".

That description had a limitation: file paths can provide navigation, but cannot substitute for the resource task graph. A directory name cannot establish when a task is created, nor can a package name prove that external CCM initialization has already occurred in the same branch. The early notes had no configuration samples, no excerpts of task edges, and did not use the results of a run to fill these gaps.

At the time, only three arrangements were on the table. Handle external CCM first; schedule user plugins after the built-in plugins finish; or always create a user-plugin task regardless of the configuration state. The third option appeared to require the least effort, because graph construction would have one fewer condition, and whether to return could simply be decided at execution time.

It was soon shelved. Without an Addons configuration, the task has no clear target; if a node is still left in the graph, later investigators will not be able to distinguish "there is no plugin work" from "there is an empty task". This was not a failure diagnosis for a particular environment, but a concern about the meaning of the task graph. The first version therefore made only one narrow decision: reject unconditional creation of a user-plugin task.

Giving external CCM priority was not settled at the time either. The only argument in its favor was that external components seemed to need preparation first, which was not enough to explain why user plugins should wait. The bigger issue is it completely sidestepped the question of whether the user-plugin branch exists when configuration is missing.

The early main text merged "no configuration" and "configuration present but not enabled" into a single empty branch. That wording remains in the historical passages because it reflects the information available at the time; a later review found it too coarse, but the later conditions cannot simply be retroactively inserted into the original notes. The conclusion about what the old passages called "empty configuration" is now retained only as a working assumption from that time.

## The Separation Recorded in the First Round of Review

The review did not require the entire addon processing to be drawn as an end-to-end flow; it only required first breaking down an overly broad phrase: "enter the addons flow". This phrase may mean only that the processing entry point was reached, or it may be read as meaning that a user plugin task already exists; the two meanings are different.

An addendum changed the review sequence to four steps. First check whether the Addons configuration object exists; once it does, check whether it is enabled; then check which stage the user plugin operation is in; finally confirm which stage the external CCM initialization resumes from. This sequence is not intended to establish the same set of prerequisites for every addon, but to separate creation conditions from relative position.

The original record did not preserve the enabled field name, default value, or configuration structure, so this layer did not make up any field explanations. What remains here is the check target that could be determined at the time, not a complete configuration description. Embedded plugins, user-provided plugins, and external CCM are often listed side by side in a single paragraph; that does not mean they have the same creation conditions.

An old note contained a very short sentence: "Once the addons flow is entered, there will be a user plugin task." It was later marked as no longer adopted. It conflated the processing entry point with task creation. Another old suggestion was to first observe the final state after the external CCM initialization; if there was no obvious anomaly, there was no need to list user plugin work separately.

The latter suggestion was also not retained as operational guidance. The final state cannot show whether the user plugin task was scheduled, skipped, or never added to the task graph. At the time, it was only intended to shorten the troubleshooting steps and cannot be used to determine relative order. The review retained the annotation next to this old suggestion: checking the final state first can narrow the scope of suspicion, but cannot replace verification of the intermediate task.

Meeting side notes once described the external CCM as "something around addon processing" and suggested waiting until the scenarios were filled in before checking the ordering. This wording was suitable for recording the deferred status at the time, but did not become a formal decision. A scenario can expose a gap in a release path, but cannot define the edge between the user plugin task and the external CCM initialization.

## Scenarios were once treated as a shortcut

After the "missing Kubernetes 1.29 e2e scenario" surfaced during the same round of wrap-up, the discussion at one point sought to use it as a common entry point for the two issues. The idea was to find a 1.29 scenario that could complete cluster creation or upgrade, while also observing the addon's final state. If there was no anomaly, the ordering issue would be temporarily set aside.

This approach appeared capable of eliminating one review, but it could only show whether a path reached its final state. It would not naturally show whether the user plugin operation occurred before or after the external CCM initialization, or whether it never entered the task graph; nor would it show whether an empty task had ever been generated when no configuration object existed. A successful cluster creation cannot automatically infer the edge of an intermediate resource task.
Therefore, scenarios and ordering were not merged into a single decision. For missing scenarios, the platform and version combinations still need to be checked in the build configuration; user plugin ordering still needs to be checked against the resource task graph and integration points. The two can arise in the same release cycle, but evidence for one cannot be substituted for evidence for the other.

The quick plan from that time is still preserved here: first run the existing 1.29 scenario, and if there are no anomalies in the final addon state, leave the relative ordering of user plugins and CCM unexamined for now. This plan is now marked **obsolete**. It can help the on-call staff narrow down the possible causes, but it does not establish the conditions under which tasks exist, nor can it replace verification of ordering.

Another side note that has not been deleted says that once a stable scenario is added, the ordering issue will probably become apparent on its own. This statement was not carried forward. The value of a stable scenario lies in covering specific platform and version combinations; whether it exposes the edges for user plugins depends on the resource task paths the scenario actually traverses, and cannot be inferred from the word "stable".

## Review in 2024 and Proposals Not Adopted

The second round of revisions first corrected an overly broad statement in the original text. Entering addon processing does not mean that a user plugin task necessarily exists; at a minimum, no configuration, not enabled, and enabled should remain separate checkpoints. Here, "separate" means that they should not be combined during troubleshooting, not that this is a complete definition of all configuration fields.

Having external CCM go first was downgraded from the default plan to an unverified hypothesis. Placing user plugins after the embedded plugins finish and before external CCM initialization became the more narrowly defined candidate position. The text at the time still required further checking of the task graph and did not present the candidate position as a guarantee already verified for all callers.

There was also discussion of folding user plugins into external CCM initialization, so that callers would see only one addon stage. The argument in favor of this proposal was that it appeared to involve fewer steps. The objections were more specific: user configuration conditions would be hidden inside CCM initialization; troubleshooters would see the external component first, but would be unable to explain why user plugins appeared or why they did not. The proposal was not adopted.

Another proposal that was not adopted was to always create user plugin tasks, then have the tasks themselves return internally. This would keep the graph's shape fixed, but would not solve the problem of empty nodes having no object, merely moving the decision that should have been made during graph construction to execution time. The review considered this to leave continued room for the earlier misinterpretations.

The following old plan has not been deleted:

> First determine whether user plugins need to be processed based on the initialization result of external CCM; if there is no obvious failure, do not split out additional tasks.

It is no longer an actionable guideline. It is retained because old links still take readers to this passage; if it were simply deleted, later readers would see only the new conclusion and would not be able to tell exactly what the review in 2024 changed. The adjacent statement that "every addon has the same prerequisites" also remains as an outdated claim.

There was also a compromise proposal at the time: attach the two tasks in a fixed order first, then let the outer layer decide whether to run user plugins based on the configuration. This proposal was not adopted in the subsequent decisions. The reason was not that a fixed order was itself problematic, but that it still handled "whether to enter the graph" and "ordering within the graph" in different places, so a single reading of the task graph still did not reveal whether the user plugins had actual objects to work on.

The review also explicitly kept responsibility for missing scenarios separate from the addon integration point. Gaps in scenario coverage need to be mapped to platform and version combinations in the build configuration; resource task edges need to be verified in the task graph. Both items may appear on the release closeout checklist, but they should not share a single completion criterion simply because they are on the same checklist.

## A Counterexample and the Correction Trail

One scenario review provided a sufficiently clear counterexample: even if a scenario for a particular version eventually completed cluster creation, that only showed that the scenario had reached its outcome state. Without task nodes and configuration states in the records, it was still impossible to tell whether user plugins had run early, run late, been skipped, or never been created. The idea that "a successful scenario also proves the ordering along the way" was therefore rejected.

This correction did not diminish the value of the scenario work itself. The missing 1.29 scenarios still need to be added, and the build configuration still needs to specify concrete platform and version combinations; it is just that this completes e2e coverage work rather than explaining the resource task graph.

Another counterexample came from an earlier assessment based on directories. Someone once inferred that embedded plugins, user plugins, and external CCM could be treated as the same stage because they were all referred to as addons for short in the notes. This shorthand obscured the user plugins' own creation conditions and insertion points. After that, directory placement was no longer used as a substitute for task relationships.

The conclusion added after these counterexamples was restrained: a final state only establishes the final state; a scenario entry point only establishes the scenario entry point; only task edges establish the relative stages. The three types of records can point to what to inspect next in one another, but none can directly replace the other two.

## Navigation for the Renewed R29 Closeout

In 2025, KONE-201 brought attention back to callers that were still using this ordering. The card called for checking the actual version, entry point, and current result. This direction can help locate call sites that need review, but it did not add a new set of task rules to this page.

KONE-201 was first categorized as release-related and then moved into processing. This action indicates that the check was put back into release closeout, not that the callers' results had already been consolidated, nor that all usage sites had obtained the same result. The old records did not include a caller list, so this page also does not extrapolate from "still in use" to conclusions about specific adopters.

KONE-218 records the current public entry point Missing 1.29 e2e Scenarios. It requires verifying the platforms and versions involved in the current build configuration, and mapping missing items to specific configuration files. Putting this item into processing, which only indicates that the scoping work has begun; the existing materials do not provide a complete platform list, nor do they conclude that any particular new scenario already covers the boundary between user plugins and external CCM.

These two cards are included in the same release closeout, with each serving as navigation in a different direction. KONE-201 directs people back to the callers and entry points that still need checking; KONE-218 directs people back to the version scenarios in the build configuration. The former cannot be read as meaning that e2e coverage is complete, and the latter cannot be read as meaning that the task order has already been confirmed by the scenario.

DOC-11 is the adjacent R29 API review material, concerning the Kubernetes 1.29 defaulting compatibility boundary and GCE Upgrade Scenario Stabilization. It can be used to locate materials from the same release round, but it does not take over the decision about the user-plugin task here. When reading the two records together, do not turn the defaulting compatibility issue into a conclusion about an Addons field that is not recorded here.

The meeting addendum also warned about an order that is easy to get wrong: do not first use the name of the missing scenario to guess addon behavior, then go back to find the resource task graph. Similar names only indicate that they occur in the same release window, but they cannot indicate that the execution paths are the same. For ordering issues, first determine whether the user-plugin operation is scheduled; for coverage issues, first determine whether the build configuration lists that platform/version combination.

## Currently Adopted Task Relationship

After considering the original sticky note, the review breakdown, the scenario counterexamples, the 2024-year review, and this round of re-scoping, the current decision is consolidated as:

The resource task graph for `WithResources` follows the publicly stated order `ensure custom addons -> ensure external CCM`: run `addons.EnsureUserAddons` after the embedded plugin completes and before the external CCM initialization, and schedule this operation only when the Addons configuration is non-nil and enabled.

This decision fixes only a local relationship. It places the user-plugin operation after the embedded plugin completes and before the external CCM initialization; it also makes a configuration object that is non-nil and enabled the scheduling condition. If no configuration object exists or the configuration is not enabled, this operation should not be scheduled under the same condition.

The "only" here refers to the scheduling condition for user plugin operations, not to folding the existence or initialization eligibility of the external CCM or the conditions for other addons into the Addons configuration. After the user plugin branch ends, the resource task graph continues to the relative phase of CCM; this does not mean that the external CCM is created because the user configuration exists.

This decision also does not retroactively recast the candidate placement from 2023 as an implementation that had already been confirmed at the time. The value of the early materials lies in preserving why unconditional graph construction was initially ruled out and why having the external CCM go first was not accepted. The current relationship emerged from the subsequent, step-by-step separation of creation conditions, relative phases, and counterexample scenarios.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> EmbeddedPluginsComplete
    EmbeddedPluginsComplete --> CheckAddonsConfiguration
    CheckAddonsConfiguration --> ScheduleUserPlugins: non-nil and enabled
    CheckAddonsConfiguration --> ContinueToCCMPhase: configuration missing or not enabled
    ScheduleUserPlugins --> ContinueToCCMPhase
    ContinueToCCMPhase --> ExternalCCMInitialization
    ExternalCCMInitialization --> [*]
```

"Continue to the CCM phase" in the diagram only means that after the user plugin check ends, the resource task graph connects to the position relative to the external CCM. It does not collapse missing configuration and CCM's own initialization check into the same branch, nor does it mean that all behavior of the external CCM when the configuration is missing has already been defined in this diagram.

When reviewing cases where user plugins did not run, first check separately whether the Addons configuration object exists and whether it is enabled, then inspect the task relationships at the integration point for user plugin operations. Even if the external CCM is observed to have completed or to show no obvious issues, this still does not justify skipping the first two checks; that is only the final observation from another phase.

When reviewing cases where Kubernetes 1.29 has no corresponding e2e entry point, follow KONE-218 to check the platform and version combinations in the build configuration. Both checks can appear together in the R29 wrap-up, but the result of one must not be written up as proof of the other. In particular, a normal result from creating a cluster must not be taken to mean that the relative phases of user plugins and the external CCM have already been confirmed by e2e coverage.

## What this page does not yet establish

Missing 1.29 e2e Scenarios has not fleshed this out into a platform list on this page. The existing material only supports checking for missing combinations in the build configuration; it cannot confirm specific platforms, versions, or CCM variants. KONE-201 also only outline how to check the caller, actual version, entry point, and current result; this page has no caller results table.

If a scenario entry point is found later, first determine whether it goes through the resource task path involving custom plugins and external CCM, then decide whether it can serve as observational evidence for this boundary. If only the final cluster state is visible, only that final state can be recorded; if only a version combination in the build configuration is found, only the scenario entry point can be recorded. Neither observation can replace confirmation of the task edges.

Likewise, if a caller is found to still be using the old integration method, first check its actual version and entry point, then determine whether it falls within the user plugin path discussed here. The caller's name, release category, or card status is not sufficient to show that it has already run through the current task relationships.

The adjacent question has still not been split out: exactly which platform and version combinations are involved in the scenarios missing from the build configuration. It remains here because the old records have long grouped scenarios and ordering together, and readers will reach that question from this page; however, it has not become evidence for ordering on this page, nor has any conclusion been reached here that the scenarios are complete.

## Archived old examples

### No anomalies in the final state

Early on, an instance of addon processing with no obvious anomalies was taken to mean that having external CCM go first was also fine. That record contained no configuration state, task nodes, or intermediate ordering, so it was later retained only as an example of a misjudgment and cannot serve as a basis for current decisions.

This example shows why the earlier investigation was insufficient, not that the final state has no value. The final state can help determine whether a particular scenario has finished, but it cannot by itself answer whether the user plugin appeared in the resource task graph, nor whether it preceded external CCM.

### Handle them uniformly if the directory names are the same

Another old example referred to embedded plugins, user plugins, and external CCM all as addons, and on that basis assumed that a single stage was enough. This wording made the notes very short, but obscured the conditions for creating user plugins and their insertion point. It remains in the appendix to prevent old links from once again leading readers to interpret directory membership as task relationships.

This claim was later overturned not because these objects were entirely unrelated, but because the types of relationships differed. They can appear around the same release processing, but whether user plugin operations enter the task graph depends on their own configuration conditions; their relative stages must also be determined by task relationships, which cannot be replaced by a shared directory label.

### Add a version scenario and verify the ordering while at it

At one point, a 1.29 scenario capable of completing cluster creation was treated as a shared entry point for both pieces of work. The two have since been separated: the scenario can help check whether the version-specific scenario exists, but it cannot show the resource task edges on its own. This old example is retained because, after KONE-218 was taken up again, the same misreading could still resurface through the old records.

The quick approach at the time was to run the existing scenario first, then decide whether the tasks needed to be split. It was appealing as a way to streamline on-site troubleshooting, but it did not record the configuration state or task nodes, so it could not serve as a basis for determining the order. It is now treated only as a shortcut tried in the past, not as an alternative to release finalization.

### All addons share a single set of prerequisites

This claim once appeared in a review side note but was not carried forward. The scheduling conditions for user plugins and the initialization conditions for external CCM cannot be automatically combined just because both are discussed as addons. The old side note did not contain enough information to define the complete conditions for each object; its mistake was to smooth over unknown differences prematurely.

This example is retained to explain why the current decision describes only the local conditions and relative order of user plugin operations. It does not extend to a unified lifecycle for the entire addon directory, nor does it make any platform coverage decisions in place of scenario configuration.

Follow-up reviews still start with user plugin integration for `pkg/addons/ensure.go`, then follow the resource task graph to confirm the relative phase of external CCM; the 1.29 scenario is traced through KONE-218 to the build configuration. What is preserved here is the progression of the R29 requirements from a conflated write-up, through deferral, to a narrowed decision, and this page still has no conclusion on the specific platforms and versions for the missing scenarios.

# R29 Defaulting Compatibility Proposal

The discussion of the default version for R29 cannot focus on the version number alone. GCE Upgrade Scenario Stabilization must be retained, but the discussion also mixes together cloud provider selection, control plane scheduling, and whether machine-controller is present. If these are collapsed into a single "upgrade to 1.29" switch, it will be hard to explain later whether a given scenario involves a version incompatibility or whether defaulting changed the objects being deployed.

Start by considering three approaches:

1. Switch all configured cloud providers as part of the version change;
2. Let the version baseline define only the supported range, and determine the cloud provider, control plane constraints, and machine-controller separately;
3. Continue requiring callers to set each option explicitly, without introducing new defaults yet.

Leaning toward the second approach. It requires broader changes, but keeps GCE Upgrade Scenario Stabilization as a separate item to verify. The first looks simpler to implement, but would hide exceptional configurations and scheduling differences in the same branch; the third leaves no verifiable default boundary for R29.

`pkg/templates/machinecontroller/cloudprovider_specs.go` is the current starting point for tracing cloud provider template relationships; the file belongs to the `machinecontroller` package. No conclusions about implementation responsibilities are being drawn from the path at this stage; it is listed only as a location to inspect when reviewing the generation rules later.

I suggest first writing a scenario matrix: standard cloud providers, explicitly using no cloud provider, control plane nodes, and stable GCE upgrades. In each cell, record only whether a default appears and which object is responsible for generating it; do not treat a single successful upgrade as a substitute for the full set of conclusions.

If the matrix cannot distinguish these conditions, abandon the defaulting attempt and return to explicit caller selection; retain the stable GCE scenario at the original entry point for continued verification.

# R29 Defaulting Compatibility Plan

The initial draft described R29 as a version switch, which was too coarse. A closer review found at least three distinct concerns being raised in the same place: which Kubernetes versions the compatibility baseline allows, whether the cloud provider changes the default deployment method, and what scheduling constraints control-plane nodes should have. GCE Upgrade Scenario Stabilization is simply subject to all of these conditions at once and should not be used in place of defining the boundaries.

The previously considered "switch everything with the version" approach remains here as an option we did not adopt. Its benefit is a smaller configuration surface for callers; the problem is that special-case configurations can only be made to work with extra overrides, and debugging would conflate the version gate, provider type, and node role. At the other extreme, "set everything explicitly" can avoid unexpected changes but would leave the default version of R29 without a clear meaning.

This revision instead starts by breaking the review down by object:

| Object | What to confirm in this review | What this review will not decide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kubernetes version | Which range serves as the compatibility baseline | Each caller's upgrade schedule |
| Cloud provider configuration | Which configurations qualify for default behavior | Internal implementation details of special-case providers |
| Control-plane nodes | Whether default scheduling constraints should be expressed separately | Specific workload placement policies |
| machine-controller | When defaulting should affect it | Ownership of the template file implementation |

`pkg/templates/machinecontroller/cloudprovider_specs.go` remains the starting point for examining the connections around the cloud provider templates. The file header confirms that it belongs to the `machinecontroller` package; this is enough for reviewers to start looking there for template declarations, but not enough to attribute all R29 decisions to this file. The initial draft's implication that "changing this is enough to cover the upgrade scenarios" should be removed.

At a minimum, this plan calls for defining the version baseline as an independent rule, then establishing separate conditions for provider defaulting, control-plane taints, and machine-controller. The review will accept only combinations whose conditions can be traced to their source, not inferences such as "the GCE upgrade reported no errors, so other providers are safe too."

GCE Upgrade Scenario Stabilization is still retained, but its records should have two columns: the stage at which execution stopped, and whether any downloadable artifacts were left. That way, even if a scenario fails, we can distinguish between an entry-point issue, an execution-stage issue, and missing artifacts; no material available so far establishes that any of these has occurred.

The rollback criteria have also been revised: rather than rolling back on any upgrade difference, stop using the new provider behavior as the default and return to explicit selection when the version baseline and provider defaulting cannot be explained separately. This rollback must not also change how control-plane constraints and machine-controller are handled.

Two concrete checks are still outstanding: which platforms and versions in the configuration fall within the compatibility range, and which stages and artifacts the stable GCE upgrade entry point actually provides.
versions.change_summary: Separated the version and defaulting boundaries after review

# R29 Defaulting Compatibility Plan

R29 This round no longer treats "defaulting" as the name of a single change. The early draft tried to use one version switch to control the provider, the control plane, and machine-controller, which looked concise during review but in practice left two questions that could not be answered: why a particular default object appears, and whether to check the version conditions or the generation conditions first when GCE Upgrade Scenario Stabilization fails.

The second version already separated the objects, but the wording still suggested that all the work could be done at a single template location. `pkg/templates/machinecontroller/cloudprovider_specs.go` can only serve as a starting point for understanding the relationships among cloud provider templates; it belongs to the `machinecontroller` package and is suitable for checking local declarations and adjacent templates, not for determining where responsibility for the entire R29 policy lies. Subsequent verification can start from this path, without treating the path name as evidence for a decision.

This round lays out the original candidate approaches again:

- **Unified version switch.** All configured providers switch to the same default behavior with the Kubernetes version, with the control-plane constraints and machine-controller also tied to that switch. This approach has been abandoned. It reduces the configuration surface but cannot represent the state where "the version meets the baseline, but a particular provider should still be treated as an exception".
- **All choices made explicitly by callers.** No R29 default behavior is added. This approach can avoid migration risks, but the compatibility window would remain only in the documentation, and callers would still have to guess individually which combinations have been accepted by the release train.
- **Independent conditions.** The version baseline, provider defaulting, the default control-plane taint, and whether machine-controller is deployed each have their own conditions; GCE Upgrade Scenario Stabilization is used to check their combined results, not to work backward from those results to define the rules. This is the approach being taken forward in this round.

The last approach does not mean redesigning every cloud configuration. What needs to be established here is the order in which conditions are evaluated: first confirm whether the cluster version is within the compatibility range of R29, then determine whether the provider belongs to the set that defaults to external; the control-plane taint is an independent node-role default; whether machine-controller is deployed is still determined by its own exception conditions. The override entry points that callers need must remain available and must not be removed just because defaulting is introduced.

The boundaries currently adopted are as follows: the Kubernetes compatibility baseline is `Kubernetes 1.27-1.29`: at 1.29 and above, configured cloud providers default to external except for explicit None and VMware Cloud Director, the control plane defaults only to `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule`, and None does not deploy machine-controller by default.

This statement replaces the initial draft's conclusion that "upgrading to 1.29 triggers a uniform switch". It also explains the role of GCE Upgrade Scenario Stabilization: this scenario should verify that configured standard cloud providers follow the expected default path within the baseline, without mistaking None, VMware Cloud Director, or control-plane scheduling behavior for side effects of GCE. GCE is not a synonym for exception rules, and it is certainly not the sole evidence for whether machine-controller appears.

Explicit None is particularly easy to overlook in review records. It must not be treated as an unspecified provider, nor may it be overridden by the external default just because the version has reached 1.29. Another item that is easily conflated is the control-plane taint: it only describes the default constraints for control-plane nodes and must not be written up as a scheduling policy for all nodes or all workloads. Both need separate entries in the scenario table, otherwise a single rendering difference will be attributed to three causes at once.

The verification entry point for the stable GCE upgrade is now recorded in KONE-219. Execution records should retain only two comparable pieces of information: the stage where the failed run stopped, and whether that run produced a downloadable artifact. When no result is available, do not fill in "upgrade passed" or "artifact missing"; the entry point itself and the result are two different kinds of records. KONE-202 is used to continue checking the platforms and versions covered by the compatibility scope and to map missing items back to specific configuration locations. The card later completed the materials review and moved to In Progress, but this still does not mean that all scenarios have conclusions.

To avoid turning the review semantics into a generic test table, only four groups of minimal combinations need to be checked in this round: configured standard providers within the baseline, explicit None, VMware Cloud Director, and nodes with the control-plane role. For each group, check the version conditions, provider default results, default node constraints, and machine-controller results separately; do not infer results for the other three groups from "one group passed". The stable GCE upgrade can serve as one actual entry point for the standard provider group, but it does not replace the other groups.

The rollback scope should also remain narrow. If verification cannot explain the version baseline and provider defaulting separately, first withdraw the newly added default external selection and restore explicit caller selection; do not use this as an opportunity to rewrite the control-plane taint, and do not let None receive machine-controller. If the issue appears only at the stable GCE upgrade entry point, first record the stage and artifacts, then determine whether it affects this defaulting rule. This keeps the rollback action tied to a known object, rather than using a single upgrade failure to invalidate the entire compatibility baseline.

The remaining work is not to add another layer of rules, but to align the platform/version gaps in the scenario table with KONE-202 and complete the actual stage and artifact records for KONE-219. Until then, the plan can be used as an interface boundary, but the stable GCE execution results that have not yet been verified must not be written up as evidence for release.
versions.change_summary: Finalize the compatibility boundary and narrow the fallback scope

# Canal Parameters and Selector Troubleshooting Tree

Start with the release artifact; don't change the network interface name first. When thecurrentsite report says Canal selected the wrong network interface, retain the manifest rendered for that run, then compare it with the interface parameters in the input. If the artifact hasn't changed, the issue isn't runtime interface selection.

The tentative view at the time was: as long as an explicit interface is provided, Flannel will use it directly. The case where a regex parameter is also present has not been ruled out. Empty values are especially tricky: they look like "not passed," but may also be treated as a set parameter during generation. Don't conflate these two kinds of blank input: no value in the release input and an empty selector received at the task entry point may not go through the same processing path.

Troubleshooting order:

```text
Canal network issue
├─ Does the rendered artifact exist?
│  ├─ No: stop at the release input; don't chase node logs yet
│  └─ Yes: inspect the interface-related entries in ConfigMap
├─ Does the input contain both an interface name and a regex?
│  ├─ Yes: record the original values; don't infer the override order from the runtime result
│  └─ No: continue with the single parameter
└─ Does e2e lack a selector?
   ├─ Yes: first confirm whether it should be rejected
   └─ No: retain the selector as-is and reproduce
```

Handling an empty e2e selector hasn't been decided. In an old artifact, one task failed to actually select a scenario, but it wasn't possible to tell at the time whether the caller hadn't passed a value or the generator had let the empty value through. Don't make the task pass by arbitrarily filling in a selector; that would erase the original input boundary.

The ConfigMap's `data` is one of the objects to retain in this round, but seeing only the key doesn't show that subsequent containers will necessarily use it as expected. Save the input, the ConfigMap fragment, and the task output separately first; then decide whether to follow the network path or the scenario-selection path.

`pkg/addons/ensure.go` was an entry point frequently consulted during the investigation. Record it here only as a locator; don't use it to determine which layer is responsible for writing the parameter, and don't attribute the selector issue to this file.

To add: obtain a release artifact containing both an interface name and a regex, confirm whether empty parameters and default parameters follow the same path, and find another task-generation result with an empty selector.

# Canal Parameter and Selector Troubleshooting Tree

This old record originally treated Canal network interface issues as node-side problems. A later review found that checking the rendered manifests first saved time. The actual interface names on the node still matter, but they cannot tell us what the release inputs ultimately became. If values are manually changed and the task rerun during the release window, a working interface afterward only shows that the new task can run; it does not explain where the original task's parameters went.

## Early approach, kept here for reference

An early on-call note said: "IFACE takes precedence if non-empty; regex is only a fallback." This statement had no source and did not cover the case where both values were supplied. It once led the investigation straight to the container environment of kube-flannel, where seeing an environment variable was taken to mean that the input had taken effect.

The usual sequence at the time was:

```text
Notice the node selected the wrong interface
  → Log in to the node and check interfaces
  → Manually change release values
  → Rerun
```

The third step must not be performed before saving the manifests. Even if manually changing the values restores service, it leaves no way to distinguish whether the difference came from parameter precedence, template writes, or the node environment. The old handoff's conclusion that "the node is already using the right interface" describes, at most, the behavior at the final layer. It cannot replace the earlier rendering records.

This assessment is now marked obsolete. It is being kept because some people still follow this sequence. It may happen to work in a case with a single interface name, but it does not establish whether a regex also entered the release inputs, or whether empty strings had already been normalized before reaching the generator.

## Field notes from the review

The review started with a downloadable release artifact. The Canal manifests contained ConfigMap; the interface-related content was not in the workload names. Check `data` in ConfigMap first, then the container section of kube-flannel, to connect the rendered keys and values with the injection result. The aim here is not to explain every field, but to distinguish two failures: "the input did not reach the manifests" and "the input arrived, but the result of consuming it was not as expected."

One counterexample recorded in this review: the container environment alone cannot be used to reconstruct the original release inputs. Environment variables may come from transformations during rendering. Whether the original parameters included both an interface name and a regex still requires checking the inputs and ConfigMap. The earlier claim that "seeing the container variable means IFACE has overridden it" was therefore withdrawn.

Another counterexample came from a rerun with missing artifacts. The node behaved normally after the rerun, but the old task's manifests had not been saved. This result cannot serve as evidence of override behavior: it neither compared the old and new inputs nor retained the differences between the two renderings. The review record marks it only as a new task after recovery, no longer as verification of the original issue.

Use the following tree to identify where to stop:

```text
Canal selects the wrong interface after release
│
├─ No corresponding rendered manifests
│  └─ Stop: obtain the release artifacts first; node-side results cannot replace them
│
├─ Manifests exist, but ConfigMap has no interface-related content
│  └─ Go back to the generation inputs; do not change kube-flannel runtime parameters
│
├─ ConfigMap has a value, but no corresponding result is visible in the container
│  └─ Record ConfigMap and the workload section; inspect the adjacent injection links
│
└─ ConfigMap and the container side both match expectations, but the node is still abnormal
   └─ Only then check node interfaces and runtime selection
```

The stop points in the tree only prevent overwriting the evidence; they do not mean implementation responsibility has been identified. `pkg/addons/ensure.go` can be used to inspect adjacent relationships on the addon side. This review did not infer who was responsible for writing values from filenames, nor did it turn unconfirmed call relationships into conclusions.

## The separate selector investigation

An empty e2e selector must not be mixed with a Canal issue in a single rerun. The former concerns the boundary at the scenario-selection entry point; the latter concerns rendering and injection of addon parameters. Some people previously treated an empty selector as shorthand for "run everything." When reviewing the previous round's artifacts, we found no record sufficient to support that interpretation.

The operating procedure is therefore: stop automatic submission when the selector is empty. Retain the task inputs and generated scenario information. If the task has already entered execution, do not overwrite the original value with a default selector and retry. It can only be treated as equivalent to "select all" if there is material showing that this entry point treats an empty value as a valid default. The available material is not sufficient yet.

If the selector was originally non-empty but the generated result is empty, do not label that an "empty selector" issue either. An input was supplied in that case; the question is in the selection process or generated result, not whether the entry point received a value. Record the original selector alongside the generated result, so that someone later seeing only the empty result does not mistakenly conclude that the caller omitted the value.

## Review notes

A simple challenge came up in review: if an empty selector really means everything, why do we still need to record the original selector? This is not an implementation conclusion, just a reminder not to present missing input as a broader test scope.

Another question was: if the relevant variable is already present in the container, can we skip ConfigMap? The answer is still no. The container section only shows that a particular result is visible at that layer. It cannot replace the release inputs, nor can it show which set of parameters produced the content in ConfigMap.

## Items not yet worked through

- When both an interface name and a regex are supplied, another artifact is needed for comparison to check how they are retained in the release inputs.
- This review has not established where an empty selector is rejected.
- If both issues occur in the same release task, preserve the Canal manifests first, then handle the selector; do not use one rerun to verify both issues.
- If an old task has already been rerun with values filled in, note that its original inputs can no longer be determined from that run's result.

# Canal Parameters and Selector Troubleshooting Tree

R29 These two types of anomalies often appear together: after deployment, Canal does not use the expected network interface, or the e2e submission contains an empty selector. They can occur in the same deployment task, but the same rerun cannot prove that both have recovered. The Canal track must retain the deployment inputs, rendered manifest, the kube-flannel snippet, and node behavior; the selector track must retain the original selector and the task generation result. Separate the two sets of evidence first so that subsequent judgments do not overwrite each other.

For on-call triage, continue using the tree below. "Stop" in the tree does not mean that the failure has been located; it means that continuing to change parameters will erase the original boundary.

```text
Symptom: Canal network interface does not match expectations, or e2e submission contains an empty selector
│
├─ First determine which track applies
│  ├─ Only Canal is anomalous
│  │  └─ Enter A
│  ├─ Only the selector is empty
│  │  └─ Enter B
│  └─ Both occur simultaneously
│     └─ First fix A's manifest, then save B's task inputs; do not combine the reruns
│
├─ A. Canal
│  ├─ The rendered manifest for this run is missing
│  │  └─ Stop: produce the missing artifact; do not log in to the node to change parameters
│  ├─ The manifest contains no network-interface-related ConfigMap content
│  │  └─ Check the deployment inputs; do not infer the inputs from the container environment at this point
│  ├─ ConfigMap has content, but there is no corresponding result on the container side
│  │  └─ Save both snippets and check injection adjacency
│  └─ Both sides match expectations, but node behavior is still incorrect
│     └─ Then check the node's actual interfaces and runtime selection
│
└─ B. selector
   ├─ The original input is empty
   │  └─ Stop automatic submission; save the generated result and do not add a default selector
   ├─ The original input is non-empty, but the generated result is empty
   │  └─ Fix the input and generated result and handle this as a selection-path anomaly
   └─ Both the original input and generated result are non-empty
      └─ This is not an empty-selector rejection; return to the specific scenario issue
```

`pkg/addons/ensure.go` can serve as an inspection point for addon adjacency, but do not attribute the selector anomaly to it merely because the filename contains addons. This path was opened frequently in old troubleshooting notes; what it is actually suited to answer is the object relationship near the Canal manifest. The selector rejection point has not been located by this document.

---

## The network-interface wording first recorded in the year 2023

The earliest record described the issue very simply: an explicit network interface name takes precedence, and the regex is only a fallback when no explicit network interface name is available. That was a statement written from memory during a handoff, without the same rendered artifact attached, and it did not account for input in which both parameters are present.

The sequence at the time was to log in to the node to check the interfaces first, then go back and change the release values. This sequence appeared to work in a few scenarios, so it was later copied into on-call notes. The problem is that node interfaces only show what is visible at runtime, not what was actually received during rendering. Once the release values were changed manually, the original override relationships were lost as well.

The original wording of the old guidance is preserved below to help identify historical records:

> When IFACE is not empty, regex can be ignored; if the target interface is visible on the node, the release parameters can be considered to have taken effect.

This guidance has been deprecated. It provided no evidence for cases where both inputs were supplied, and it did not distinguish between empty, omitted, and invalid parameters. The bigger issue is it treated the final node behavior as the sole criterion for judging the entire release pipeline. If you see old records quoting this statement in the future, do not use it as a reason to skip the manifest.

## Two marginal notes on an on-call page from 2023

Later, a handoff page contained just two sentences: get the artifact first; do not infer inputs from container variables. They were brief, but they changed the troubleshooting order.

"Get the artifact" means the manifest generated for that particular release, not an arbitrary object captured from an already running cluster. If the manifest contains nothing related to network interfaces, continuing to investigate containers or nodes will not provide an answer; conversely, only when the manifest contains relevant content but there is no corresponding result on the container side is it worth saving the snippets from both sides side by side.

"Do not infer inputs from container variables" does not mean container snippets have no value, either. The container environment is the visible result after injection, but it cannot by itself prove whether the original input was an interface name, a regex, or an empty value. In one old record, visible variables were treated directly as input values, and a node anomaly was then interpreted as Flannel ignoring the parameters. Subsequent checks did not support that interpretation.

From then on, at least four items had to be retained on site in this order: release inputs, rendered ConfigMap, the kube-flannel snippet in the workload, and node-side behavior. The first two answer "Was it written in?", the third answers "What was injected?", and only the last answers "What was selected at runtime?" If the first or second item is missing, stop on the release side; do not fabricate a seemingly reasonable parameter combination just to continue troubleshooting.

## Review in 2024: a comparison with no conclusion

The review once attempted to put the interface name and the regex separately into comparison inputs, then determine which overrode which based on node behavior. This attempt failed. It was not that the node reported no errors, but that the rendered content from the same run had not been retained. In the end, only the runtime results were visible, so it was impossible to confirm exactly how the two inputs had been retained during generation.

The practical lesson from this was not that a particular parameter always takes precedence, but this: without the manifest, do not claim that precedence has been verified. Treating a missing rendered artifact as an ordinary test failure and rerunning will cause the next result to obscure the previous inputs. A rerun can restore service, but the new task after recovery cannot retroactively prove the parameter relationships in the original task.

During review, another seemingly useful snippet also came up: kube-flannel Related variables appeared in the container. Based on this, someone initially said that IFACE had already been covered. The review required placing this snippet alongside ConfigMap, after which the conclusion was withdrawn. Variables visible in the container can, at most, show that a value exists at some layer after injection; they cannot show whether ConfigMap contains the expected keys, nor whether the release input included another set of parameters.

Therefore, the Canal path needs to distinguish three different failure surfaces:

```text
The release input exists, but the manifest does not show the expected content
  → This is still a rendering-side issue; do not jump to the node

The manifest already has content, but the kube-flannel snippet does not show the corresponding result
  → Record both objects and continue investigating injection adjacency

Both the manifest and the container snippet match expectations, but the node still selects the wrong interface
  → Only then proceed to the node's actual interface and runtime selection
```

These three branches have no common "quick fix." In particular, for the second branch, do not directly modify container parameters in an attempt to recover; that would conflate the manifest-layer record with the runtime override as a single result.

## 2024 Another failure path that year: treating an empty selector as all

That same year, an empty selector appeared at an e2e entry point. Someone interpreted the empty value as shorthand for "select all scenarios," added a commonly used selector, and resubmitted. The task being able to continue does not mean the empty value was valid; it only means that the newly added value worked.

That record did not preserve the relationship between the original selector and the scenario-generation result, so the semantics of the empty value cannot be inferred from it. Nor is it suitable as an example of "the empty selector was handled normally." The original task's input boundary had already been overwritten by the value-addition action, so it can only be labeled as a new trial after recovery.

Here, the two empty-result cases must be separated: the original selector itself being empty and the selector being non-empty but producing no results are not the same thing. The former is first of all an input-boundary issue, while the latter indicates that input existed but did not produce the expected scenarios. Calling the latter an "empty selector" as well would send troubleshooting to validation first and instead skip the generation process.

At a minimum, the on-call record should contain two items: the original selector value and the scenarios generated by the task. When the original value is empty, stop automatic submission; when the original value is non-empty but the result is empty, preserve both and handle it as an exception in the selection path. Any submission after adding a value counts as a separate task and must not overwrite the original record.

## Abandoned quick recovery method

The following section was once written on the emergency recovery page. It is now explicitly no longer applicable, but is retained for people reviewing old handoffs:

```text
When the node interface is wrong: directly modify the NIC parameters and rerun;
when the selector is empty: add the most recently usable selector;
as long as the task completes, mark both items as resolved.
```

The problem is not that the corrected value is necessarily ineffective, but that it treats "the recovered new task" as "validation of the original input." This loses two types of information: how the original Canal parameters entered the manifest, and exactly where the empty selector was accepted or rejected.

If the release window really requires recovery, a corrected, separate task can be initiated; the original task must still retain its original values and the results generated at the time. For Canal, the corrected task's manifest must also be kept separate from the original manifest; do not use the new manifest to fill in missing artifacts from the old task. Even if they differ by only one parameter, the two sets of materials were produced under different conditions at the time.

## Review Excerpts and Revisions

Two counterexamples were repeatedly raised during the verification review.

The first counterexample was: if the relevant variables are already visible in the container, can we consider both ConfigMap and the release inputs correct? The answer is no. The container snippet can show the visible state after injection, but it cannot replace the upstream inputs and rendered content. This invalidates the statement in the old notes that "container variables can serve as the sole criterion."

The second counterexample concerns an empty selector: if the system treats an empty value as all, why must the original selector still be saved during troubleshooting? This question did not establish a conclusion about an alternative implementation, but it was enough to prevent silently expanding an empty value into a full test run. Once an empty value is filled in with a commonly used selector, the original boundary is lost.

The review also noted that `pkg/addons/ensure.go` is not a universal entry point. It is appropriate to open it when the Canal manifest and its adjacency to the addon need further confirmation; the point at which the selector is rejected should not be inferred from this path. The path is for navigation, not for presenting unknown implementation responsibilities as established facts.

## Current Triage Actions

For a Canal anomaly, first ask whether the rendered manifest from that run is available. If not, stop at the release artifacts; do not log in to a node to change parameters. This does not require the on-call person to explain the addon's full implementation or check all callers first; the current question is whether the parameters were rendered, and without an artifact there is no basis for further assessment.

If the artifact exists, find Canal's ConfigMap. If it contains no network-interface-related content, return to the release inputs. For this branch, only write "the current manifest does not show the expected content"; do not state that a particular runtime component has already discarded the parameters.

If ConfigMap already contains content, then inspect the kube-flannel snippet. If there is no corresponding result on the container side, the question shifts from "whether the input exists" to "how the manifest content is injected." Preserving the original snippet containing the keys, values, and their enclosing object is more useful than writing "the parameters look correct." Only if both the manifest and container snippet match expectations but the node is still abnormal should you check the node interfaces and runtime selection; new findings on the node side explain only the final layer and do not automatically prove that there were no differences in the preceding layers.

The selector track is shorter. If the original selector is empty, stop automatic submission and save the task generation results. If the original selector is non-empty but the generation results are empty, do not group this under "empty selector rejection"; it is a different anomaly in which existing input did not produce the expected scenarios. If both the original input and generation results are non-empty, this page does not go into further detail; return to the specific e2e scenario issue.

When both anomalies occur in the same round, first preserve Canal's inputs and manifest, then save the original selector value and generation results. As long as either track still lacks the minimum on-site records, do not use a single combined rerun to draw a conclusion about the other track.

## Current Requirements

The Canal parameter rendering contract is `IFACE=eth1; IFACE_REGEX=en.*; FLANNELD_IFACE_REGEX`: the first two values are written to the `data` mapping in ConfigMap, and kube-flannel injects the corresponding environment variables from canal_iface_regex; empty parameters still retain automatic network interface selection.

This requirement specifies the order of checks for Canal parameters, from input to rendering and then to injection into kube-flannel. It does not interpret an empty selector as selecting everything by default, nor does it automatically attribute any node-side anomaly to a parameter override. The on-call action for an empty selector remains to refuse to continue automatically and retain the input and generated results.

Field records can be abbreviated using five stopping points:

1. No manifest from the current rendering run: stop at the release artifact; do not change node parameters.
2. ConfigMap does not show network interface content: stop at the release input; do not substitute container variables for the manifest.
3. The manifest has content, but the container snippet does not match: stop at the injection boundary and retain snippets from both objects.
4. Empty selector: stop at the submission entry point; do not add a default selector.
5. Both anomalies occur in the same round: first save the originals separately, then decide whether to submit two independent correction tasks.

Here, "automatic network interface selection" applies only to empty parameters. It cannot be extended to mean that execution should continue for any missing or unparseable value. When historical records do not allow empty values to be distinguished from default values, leave them unchanged and stop making inferences.

## Related issues still open

In the same round, people often ask whether rejection of an empty selector occurs before scenario generation or before submission. The available materials do not establish the location; this page retains only the checkpoints for the input and generated results. If investigation continues, start a separate record for the selector entry point rather than inserting speculation into Canal's ConfigMap branch.

Another issue that has not yet been separated out is that, when both network interface parameters appear together, an actual artifact is still needed for comparison with the saved form of the release input. Until that artifact is available, do not reinstate the earlier conclusion about "which takes precedence." The current requirements provide checkpoints for rendering and injection, but do not mean that all combinations have been verified here.

## Old appendix: initial troubleshooting excerpt

Below is a one-page excerpt circulated early on; its wording is outdated:

> First check the interfaces on the node. If the interface name matches expectations, there is no configuration problem; if it does not, adjust IFACE and rerun. Reserve regex for special environments.

This section does not handle a missing manifest, the coexistence of two parameters, or the result of container injection, nor does it distinguish an empty parameter from an empty selector. It is still included here because old release records will reference the "check nodes first" order. When citing an old record, add the current first step alongside it: first obtain the rendered output for that run.

Another appendix states:

> When the selector is empty, first choose a common scenario and run the task.

This passage is likewise no longer applicable. It can serve as a new experiment after recovery, but it cannot replace rejecting and retaining the original empty value. If historical tasks have already been rerun this way, mark them only as "the original input can no longer be verified"; do not backfill them to say that an empty selector was handled normally.

Finally, retain one reminder: when the phrase "the parameter has taken effect" appears in the field, clarify whether it means that the input exists, ConfigMap has a value, the container environment can see it, or node selection actually succeeded. These four things can happen sequentially, or the chain can break between them. If you write them as a single success statement, the next troubleshooter will have to guess all over again.

# R29 e2e and Flatcar Verification Workflow

At R29 closeout, two related compatibility issues were first put on one page: the verbose parameter for the compiled e2e artifact, and the post-upgrade results for Flatcar Remote stat mode. Review can currently start at `test/e2e/helpers.go`, and the file is declared as `package e2e`. This serves as an initial point for tracing back; it does not establish which layer actually assembles the parameters.

The previous plan was to keep the CI wrapper, then migrate to the maintained run entry point. Comparisons should use the same compiled artifact, selector, and timeout, changing only verbose; otherwise, if the outputs differ, there is no way to tell whether the cause is the entry point, selection criteria, or logging parameters.

For Flatcar, the only record left is "regression checks on remote stat mode results after the upgrade." The lists of paths taken and paths excluded are both still incomplete; e2e output cannot be used as a substitute. The tentative sequence is:

1. Save the compiled artifact and the original run conditions.
2. Run once through the old entry point and once through the new entry point, using the same selector and timeout.
3. Change only verbose, and save the process launch arguments.
4. Make a separate list of paths taken and paths excluded for Flatcar.

If the post-migration e2e results cannot be explained, first rerun through the old entry point; Flatcar will not be restored along with e2e at this stage. TODO: Add the pre- and post-upgrade path lists, and confirm whether the old wrapper can continue to serve as a temporary reference.
