# R29 e2e and Flatcar Cross-Check Procedure

The previous version treated verbose, the old CI wrapper, and Flatcar stat mode as a single migration track, making it read as if the same entry point controlled both at once. After review, record them separately first: e2e only checks the startup conditions for the build artifact, while Flatcar only checks path changes in remote stat mode. Both issues are still being closed out in the same release cycle, but the recovery actions cannot be combined.

### e2e Comparison Sequence

The recheck point is still `test/e2e/helpers.go`; the file itself only provides the local adjacency for `package e2e`. The old record attributes verbose to the wrapper, but that is only a working hypothesis. During migration, first pin the build artifact, then keep the selector and timeout unchanged while comparing the old entry point with the maintained entry point; only when the conditions for the two runs match should changes in verbose be observed separately.

Do not reverse the order. If the selector is changed along with the entry point, the test set has already changed; if the timeout changes too, the timeout behavior cannot be attributed to verbose. Retain the startup arguments and test output for every result, so at minimum it is clear what changed in this round.

### Flatcar Path Tracking

Flatcar will no longer use e2e output as corroborating evidence. For remote stat mode after the upgrade, save the raw result first, then record separately the paths actually entered and the paths excluded. If results from the old mode can be found, compare them by path; if not, retain only the regression symptom and do not directly determine which side should be restored.

The two batches of actions are tentative: Batch 1 migrates only the e2e entry point, leaving the build artifact, selector, and timeout unchanged; Flatcar Remote stat mode is handled only in Batch 2. If an anomaly appears in Batch 2, stop at that batch first, retain the paths and raw results, and do not roll back the Batch 1 e2e comparison.

The old wrapper remains as a historical reference, but "can be restored at any time" has not been confirmed. If the e2e comparison fails, recheck against the original conditions first; if the Flatcar results are unstable, complete the path baseline first. # R29 e2e and Flatcar Cross-Check Procedure

This page is a migration record left during release closeout, not merely a parameter reference. The earliest version put the e2e build artifact, the old CI wrapper, and Flatcar Remote stat mode on one sheet; only an intermediate version split entry-point changes from remote-path changes into two batches. The old sections remain because they explain why people kept saying "results didn't match" without being able to identify which condition had changed.

```text
Old record: e2e entry point + Flatcar stat mode
             |
             v
Batched records: e2e entry-point comparison | Flatcar path record
```

## First, see what the old record left behind

`test/e2e/helpers.go` has always been the starting point for this page. The file header shows `package e2e`, so early checks naturally started there. At the time, the working hypothesis was that verbose might be passed to e2e by the old CI wrapper, while selector and timeout were inherited from the original job. This hypothesis was not treated as establishing implementation ownership; it was used only to plan the next comparison.

The migration draft for the old entry point was never actually completed. It called for saving one build artifact, running it once through the old entry point and once through the new entry point with the same selector and timeout, and then changing verbose. It did not retain the complete results from the two runs, so it could establish only the comparison order, not which parameters either entry point actually passed.

The Flatcar record stalled even earlier: after the remote stat mode upgrade, the results regressed, but the paths actually entered and the excluded paths were not fully recorded. Someone placed it alongside the e2e startup output, hoping to explain both sides with the same output; without matching remote-path evidence, that approach was later crossed out. The two issues only happened to be adjacent during the R29 closeout; they cannot share a recovery conclusion.

> Old draft: Run the old wrapper first, then migrate to the maintained entry point; if the new result differs, go back to the old entry point.
>
> [Obsolete] This sentence conflates "the old entry point can be restored" with "the new entry point changes only one condition." The old entry point later ceased to be an executable prerequisite for recovery, but keeping it helps readers understand what the early record was pointing to.

## The intermediate version's batching approach

During review, first lock down the e2e conditions. The build artifact must not be swapped during the entry-point comparison; selector and timeout must remain unchanged as well. Save the results from the old and maintained entry points separately, and record the launch parameters. Only after the first round of entry-point comparison is complete should you inspect the output differences associated with verbose. That way, even if the results differ, the difference can still be traced to the entry point or logging parameters instead of mixing in the artifact, test set, and timeout conditions.

For Flatcar, use a separate path record. Under remote stat mode, first save the raw result, then fill in two columns: the path actually entered and the excluded path. If a comparable pre-upgrade record exists, compare it item by item; without a pre-upgrade baseline, do not turn missing paths into guesses. In particular, do not keep only successful paths, because then you cannot tell whether filtering hid a change.

A stopping point separates the two batches. The first batch handles only the e2e entry point and retains the original build artifact, selector, and timeout; when it ends, save the parameters and test results. Only then should the second batch handle Flatcar Remote stat mode, keeping the entered paths, excluded paths, and what the remote side returned in its own record. If the second batch is unstable, stop subsequent Flatcar adjustments; do not undo the e2e assessment just because the two issues are close together.

## Current entry-point guidance

The compiled e2e process matching the selector accepts `-test.v -test.timeout -test.run` across three parameter categories, with timeout and selector unchanged; the deprecated legacy CI wrapper has been removed, leaving only the maintained go-test-e2e.sh entry point.

This guidance corrects the earlier assessment of the wrapper, but does not make `helpers.go` a parameter source. When checking old jobs or old screenshots, you may still see the wrapper name; that is a historical reference. The actual cross-check should start from the maintained go-test-e2e.sh entry point and continue using the saved build artifact, selector, and timeout.

Here, "unchanged" refers to the comparison conditions; it does not require the output text to be exactly the same every time. A change in entry point may alter output ordering or ancillary information; to assess verbose's impact, you still need to first confirm that the build artifact and test selection did not also change. If the conditions are not fully recorded, the results are only investigative clues and cannot be treated as proof that the migration is complete.

## Recovery boundary that remains actionable

If the e2e comparison shows a difference, do not restore the removed legacy CI wrapper. Keep the current build artifact, rerun the original selector and original timeout through the maintained entry point, and review this run's launch parameters together with the previously saved results. Do not casually replace the selector during the rerun; if it must be changed, start a separate record set and do not overwrite the original comparison.

Flatcar's recovery boundary is narrower. Once an anomaly appears, stop the second-batch actions that have not yet started, and save the raw post-upgrade results, the entered paths, and the excluded paths. Discuss restoring the old mode only if the pre-upgrade results can be matched path by path. This page still has neither a complete before-and-after-upgrade path table nor a result sufficient to serve directly as a recovery baseline; the e2e record does not fill these two gaps.

The old merged approach remains in the appendix: one run changed the entry point, inspected verbose, and observed stat mode at the same time; once it failed, all that remained was "results differ." What changed later was not the fact that the issues needed to be seen in the same release window, but the practice of treating them as one investigation chain. Next time this page is checked, first gather evidence separately in the e2e and Flatcar batches, then decide whether to continue the migration.

# Azure CCM System CA Trial Run Notes

The material at hand puts Azure CCM system CA and Kubernetes 1.29 Default Version Stabilization into the same validation round, but they should not share a results field. The former first checks whether the rendered workload has a usable certificate path; the latter must be recorded separately by tracking the values from the build artifact and stable version. This records the sample and interpretation method for the former first; the default version is only a parallel item, and no inference is drawn from the behavior of CA.

During troubleshooting, someone started from `pkg/cmd/shared.go`. The file starts with `package cmd` and a set of imports; it is more like a nearby command-side entry point and cannot replace the manifest itself. The experiment sample should still retain the rendered Azure CCM workload, the corresponding Helm values, and Kustomization. This lets the review start from the same object, rather than treating a command-layer pointer as proof that the container has loaded the certificate.

## Comparison Setup

This round is not marked "passed." No output from an actual CI run has been attached yet, so the three things—configuration exists, the value is passed in, and the container actually reads it—must be kept separate. When reviewing the rendered result, confirm the object and container first, then write down the directory path; do not infer runtime status from a single line in values. Observations for the stable version are also kept separate, so defaulting changes do not mask the certificate issue.

The finalized rendering requirements are as follows.

The Azure CCM workload's `env` list is set to `SSL_CERT_FILE=/usr/share/ca-certificates/ca-certificates.crt`, and the host `/usr/share/ca-certificates` is mounted into the container at the same path; both Helm values and Kustomization pass that CA directory.

This describes the chain formed by the same CA directory across three locations; it is not a check of any one of them. Seeing the directory only in values does not show that the workload includes the mount; seeing only the container environment variable does not show that the absolute path is readable inside the container. The rendered object should be retained as a revalidation attachment so the container settings and volume declaration can be reviewed together in the same comparison.

## Fragments to Retain During Revalidation

- The name of the rendered object, the Azure CCM container being checked, and the certificate file path exactly as written in the container environment variable.
- The value of the CA directory in Helm values and Kustomization, confirming that neither location was changed to a different directory.
- The workload output from the same CI run; if this section is missing, label it only as a rendering observation, not a runtime result.

For the next revalidation, keep the same rendering input and stable-version selection, changing only whether the host CA directory is provided. If the directory is missing but is still recorded as usable, retain the sample as a counterexample; if both the directory and path are present but there is no process-side result, it still must not be written up as having taken effect.

Kubernetes 1.29 Default Version Stabilization is used here only for cross-checking: its version value, build steps, and fallback entry point are stored separately and are not combined with the container observations for Azure CCM. If the default version changes, the CA sample can be rerun without first guessing which validation track changed the result.

# R29 Rendering and Azure Decision Record

The R29 closeout phase had two adjacent workstreams: Calico and Canal 3.27.2 Rendering, and Azure addon Kustomization. They remain in the same history because the release checks need to trace both requirements; not because they have been confirmed to share templates, manifests, or generation locations. The early records gave this distinction too little emphasis, so when consulted later, "appearing on the same page" was easily read as "being generated in the same place".

The initial working hypothesis was to file these under image changes. Both the old issue names and the call names could lead a reader to `pkg/templates/images/images.go`, while the file header also showed `package images` and an import block. This entry point was not irrelevant: starting the review from image objects was indeed more direct than searching blindly through release manifests. The problem is that it only explains where the investigation began, not that the subsequent rendered manifests or Kustomization files are determined here.

This assessment was later narrowed, not because the path had lost its value, but because it was being used to support a conclusion that went beyond the available material. The same reading entry point can lead to different targets; the same R29 work log can also contain different verification actions. The path remains in the document, with its role changed to two purposes: reviewing local declarations of image objects, and following references at the revision used at the time to trace connections to neighboring objects. It is no longer described as the source of results for Calico, Canal, or Azure addon.

## Approaches Considered at the Time

The first approach was to place all three under the images path. Its advantage was that the old investigation clues were collected in one place, with the relevant names visible on a single page; its drawback was also clear, as readers would mistake the navigation location for where the artifacts were implemented. This approach was not retained as the final organizational structure.

The second approach was to split them completely into three unconnected records. This would make it easiest to preserve the Calico, Canal, and Azure material separately, but it would erase an actual piece of context: they were brought into the closeout scope during the same round of release checks for R29. Once they were fully separated, later readers could only guess from the close timing why they had been listed together.

The third approach was a shared history with separate verification. The page retains the context of "why they entered the record at the same time", while paragraphs and review targets are separated by artifact. The decision was to adopt the third approach. Here, the shared history is only a history of requirements, not a shared workflow or shared manifests, nor shared rollback actions.

| Organizational Approach | Content Retained | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Group by the images path | Reading clues provided by old issue names and call names | Not used as a technical classification |
| Separate all three completely | Independent result records for each target | Not adopted as the primary recordkeeping approach |
| History on one page, targets separated | R29 context from the same period and verification of each artifact | Adopted |

This decision addresses record granularity, not the final status of the three targets. Further material should still be added under each respective target; establishing the shared history does not allow rendering differences, file contents, or versions that have not yet been obtained to be recorded as established facts.

## Boundaries for Listing Calico and Canal Together

Calico and Canal can be listed together on this page as "3.27.2 rendering coverage". This grouping indicates that they belong to the same round of release checks and makes it easier to find adjacent requirements when reviewing R29; it does not make Canal an alias for Calico, nor does it allow one plugin's output to substitute for verification of the other.

For Calico, the record needs to retain the corresponding workflow, the differences seen in the rendered output, and its rollback entry point. Even if only Calico results become available later, they can only establish Calico's output; they cannot also be used to state that Canal's output is already the same. Canal uses the same level of recording detail, but verification must still return to Canal's corresponding workflow, rendering differences, and rollback entry point. The two share release context, not default conclusions.

The initial draft's wording, "review the network plugins together", is retained as a record of the working order at the time, but no longer serves as a technical explanation. The purpose of that arrangement was first to confirm whether 3.27.2 coverage was included in the release checks, not to confirm that the two rendering results would necessarily be identical. Later records should express "adjacent coverage scopes" and "identical artifacts" separately.

## Separate Verification for Azure addon

The verification target for Azure addon differs from the first two. Here, return to the entry point for "Azure addon Kustomization", rerun it on a platform supported by the maintainers, and then inspect the files and versions actually generated. The Kustomization name helps locate the action, but the name alone cannot prove that the generated artifacts already exist, nor can it show that they are related to the network plugin rendering results.

Therefore, Azure addon should not use Calico or Canal rendering results to fill the gaps. Even if the three targets are discussed in the same closeout round, only Azure's own files and versions are accepted as its review results. The reverse is also true: Azure's generated files and versions cannot be interpreted as evidence that Calico or Canal rendering is complete.

This is also why the old path is retained without expanding its meaning. `pkg/templates/images/images.go` can help explain local declarations near image objects, but it does not provide the actual files generated by Azure addon Kustomization. Describing it as a unified entry point would create incorrect attribution again.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> R29SharedHistory
    R29SharedHistory --> CalicoAndCanal3272Rendering
    R29SharedHistory --> AzureaddonKustomization
    CalicoAndCanal3272Rendering --> VerifyArtifactsSeparately
    AzureaddonKustomization --> VerifyArtifactsSeparately
```

The convergence point in the diagram only indicates that both workstreams enter the closeout record for R29. It does not mean that network plugin rendering and Azure addon Kustomization use the same generation process, nor that they produce the same type of file.

## Do Not Merge Rollback Records

A shared history should not collapse rollback into a single action. When rendering differences appear on the Calico side, return to the rollback entry point for Calico's corresponding workflow; when they appear on the Canal side, use Canal's entry point. When differences appear in Azure's generated artifacts, return to the addon's Kustomization entry point to review the files and versions. These three types of records can appear next to each other on this page, but the rollback reasons and targets must remain in their respective paragraphs.

This distinction is also useful for later changes. If only one workstream changes, edits should be confined to that workstream's paragraph and should not automatically rewrite the other two. If Calico and Canal show the same type of change in the future, they can be described side by side once results exist for both sides; until then, "the same round of 3.27.2 rendering coverage" only indicates adjacency in the requirements history.

## Content Still to Be Added

What has been finalized on this page is the organizational approach and the boundaries on what can be concluded, not the specific results for the three targets. Calico's actual rendering differences have not yet been attached; Canal's actual rendering differences have not yet been attached; the specific files and versions generated by Azure addon after rerunning on a supported platform have not yet been attached either.

When adding supporting evidence later, simply update the corresponding paragraphs for Calico, Canal, and Azure separately. If there are new reference relationships involving the images path, only update its description as a reading entry point, without automatically reversing this decision to separate the targets. The R29 history remains on a single page, while rendering outputs, Azure artifacts, and each target's rollback entry point remain separate.

## How to Record the Next Review

When the next maintainer receives new material, they should specify whether they are checking Calico, Canal, or Azure addon, then include the actual workflow or Kustomization entry point, the revision used for the run, and the artifact location. Only fill in the column with new results; if outputs come from different platforms or different windows, start a separately dated record rather than overwriting the unknowns retained on this page. When none of the three has new results, do not change their status to "verified" just because the R29 closeout date is approaching.

# R29 Matrix and Network Adjustment Plan

R29 First, put Kubernetes 1.29 e2e Matrix Normalization and Azure Disk host networking into the same trial discussion. The rationale is simple: when maintainers select the 1.29 scope in the old scenarios, they have to repeatedly compare names. If the selection criteria can be consolidated, regression might also confirm that the Azure Disk network change did not remain limited to a local configuration.

There are two candidate approaches. The first is to add, alongside the existing e2e entry point, a unified selection criterion targeting 1.29; the same run would also cover Azure Disk. This reduces manual selection, but changes how the old scenario names are understood. The second leaves the selection criteria unchanged and only adds an independent scenario; the change is smaller, at the cost of maintainers still having to manually compare version ranges side by side.

The prior investigation entered through `test/e2e/tests_test.go`. Search terms in the file include `aws_default` and `install_containerd_external`. For the time being, treat this file as the scenario entry point; do not infer from that that matrix generation or Azure Disk configuration is completed here.

During the trial, rerun on platforms supported by the maintainers and compare the actual generated files and versions. For Azure Disk, check separately the configuration closure involved in the change. If the unified selection criterion makes the old scenarios indistinguishable from the 1.29 scope, or if the network check can only be completed outside this entry point, withdraw the approach of tying the two efforts together.

Not yet decided: whether host networking is worth making a fixed dimension in the matrix, or should be retained only as a local check for Azure Disk.

# R29 Matrix and Networking Adjustment Proposal

The original idea is still recorded here: since Kubernetes 1.29 e2e Matrix Normalization was going to clean up scenario selection, Azure Disk host networking could be included in the same regression cycle. That argument was convenient in the earlier discussion, because both tasks required maintainers to revisit the results of 1.29. But it is not a settled implementation plan.

At the time, the main difficulty was scenario scope. The old names gave some indication of historical coverage, but did not always make it immediately clear which combinations belonged to 1.29. The initial draft therefore leaned toward adding unified selection criteria and checking Azure Disk as well in a single e2e run. The alternative was to keep the existing selection criteria and add a separate scenario just for the networking change. The first approach consolidated selection; the second kept the old names recognizable. Neither option has enough supporting material for a firm decision yet.

The old starting point for investigation is still recorded here: `test/e2e/tests_test.go`. This review only showed that the file uses `package e2e`, with `import (` next in the file header. `aws_default` and `install_containerd_external` can help recover the context of the old scenarios, but they do not themselves identify who generates the selection criteria for 1.29, or which file owns the Azure Disk network configuration. Listing these names as the "matrix implementation location" was an overreach in the early notes.

## Original Rationale for Combining the Work

The initial draft treated "the same entry point" as a fairly strong argument: if scenarios were selected in one place, the Azure Disk checks seemed able to count as part of that round's results. That premise did not hold up on review. The scenario entry point, the files actually generated, and the set of configurations involved in the networking change cannot be treated as the same object, at least in this record.

The earlier conclusion remains recorded here: unified selection criteria may make version differences easier to assess than maintaining a series of scattered scenarios. This reflects the pain of manual selection; it should not be treated as evidence that Azure Disk checks are already covered, nor does it mean that all the old scenarios should be given the same name.

The counterexample here is that the checks address different concerns. Matrix normalization focuses on which files a run actually generates on maintainer-supported platforms and which versions they correspond to; Azure Disk host networking focuses on whether the change covers its configuration closure. Even if the former makes the scenario scope clear, it does not follow that the latter's configuration is complete. Conversely, having no omissions in the network configuration does not prove that scenario selection for 1.29 has been normalized.

## Switch to Two Reversible Trial Tracks

The recommendation is to stop treating "combining the work" as the default outcome and first separate the work by what is being examined.

For the matrix track, start with two things: keep the old scenario names for comparison; rerun the target entry point on maintainer-supported platforms and verify the files and versions actually generated. If the new selection criteria merely change names without making the coverage of 1.29 easier to identify, they should no longer be presented as normalization.

For the Azure Disk track, start with the configurations involved in the host networking change and work outward. The focus is not on whether an e2e entry point exists, but on whether any part of the related configuration remains uncovered by this change. It is not unusual for the networking checks to extend beyond the test files; that only means they should no longer be an add-on to the matrix adjustments.

The two tracks can use the same regression window, but their records must be kept separate. A single passing scenario only shows that the scenario exposed no problems in that run and cannot replace the Azure Disk configuration checks; likewise, completing a check of one configuration cannot replace the results generated for the version matrix. This split adds comparison work, but when something fails, it makes it possible to see whether the selection criteria changed the scope or the networking change left something out.

## Trade-offs Between the Options

The option that retains unified selection criteria is well suited to reducing the burden on maintainers of piecing together the 1.29 scenario scope each time. The trade-off is that the old names may lose their original usefulness as cues, especially when existing scenarios also carry cues about the platform, installation method, or version. The available material is not enough to show that all these cues can be safely collapsed.

The option that retains separate scenarios has the advantage of confining risk to the localized Azure Disk checks; the old matrix does not have to be renamed immediately. It does not solve the problem of manual selection, and the selection criteria for 1.29 may still need to be handled separately later. The smaller change does not justify calling matrix normalization complete.

There is also an intermediate approach: do not add any criteria initially, and just compare the existing scenarios in a single rerun based on the files and versions actually generated; try unified selection criteria only when the scope genuinely cannot be identified. This approach leaves room to back out, but also defers the decision on whether the entry point needs adjustment. The preference at this stage is to use it as the starting point for the next trial, rather than as a final decision.

## Stop Conditions and Open Issues

If the new selection criteria mix together the existing scenarios and the 1.29 scope, stop the matrix normalization trial and return to using the old scenario names for comparison. If the Azure Disk checks confirm that the investigation needs to extend into other configurations, stop trying to squeeze them into the same matrix change; the networking checks can still continue on their own. In either case, stopping does not mean that the other track's work is invalid.

Still unconfirmed are the exact scope of the configuration closure and whether host networking should become a long-term matrix dimension. `test/e2e/tests_test.go` remains a starting point for reviewing old scenarios, not a conclusion about ownership of these two questions. If later notes add the files and versions actually generated, the trial assessment here should be revised first, before deciding whether the selection-criteria changes are worth including in the release scope.

# Cilium Embedded Plugin Decision Record

This record was once consulted as the release confirmation page for Cilium 1.15.2. What it actually preserves is an earlier decision on how to classify the requirement: when R29 was finalized, the name "embedded plugin" was enough to send people looking for a standalone plugin directory, while the clues available at the time pointed to image-related files. The first draft therefore put heavy emphasis on the image-side starting point for reading. Looking back, that wording can no longer directly answer whether the release contents were actually loaded; it still explains why no parallel integration guide was opened for this item at the time.

## Scope of the Decision at the Time

The May discussion was not about two fully formed implementation options, but about two ways to keep the record.

- Treat Cilium 1.15.2 as an external integration item and create a separate release tracking thread;
- Keep it in the embedded plugin history for R29, with image-related locations as the starting point for reading.

The second option was adopted. The known local entry point was `pkg/templates/images/images.go`. That file is a Go module under `package images`, with the direct dependencies visible at the top of the file starting with `import (`. Based on the material available at the time, attaching the version item to this entry point first was safer than inferring a standalone implementation area from the name.

This decision did not redefine code ownership for Cilium 1.15.2, nor did it commit to image files being the sole source of the final manifest. It only decided where to keep the requirement material and where someone investigating it should start. The first draft overstated the latter point: it turned "you can start reading here" into "following this path will confirm the release contents."

## Earlier Assessment Retained in the First Draft

The old draft assumed that checking along `pkg/templates/images/images.go` would establish whether the embedded plugin shipped on the release train. That assessment did not lead to a new release strategy, but it made the later reading path appear to be the only one.

The proposal to "create a separate plugin entry point and documentation for this version" was not adopted at the time. This was not because other related locations had been proven not to exist, but because there was no material supporting separate implementation ownership for the version item. Creating a separate guide first would naturally lead readers to understand it as another maintenance area; that would have been out of proportion to the image-side clues that were all we had at the time.

The core decision in the old draft therefore remains: Cilium 1.15.2 belongs in the embedded plugin history for R29, rather than in a separate record as an external integration item. What needs to be withdrawn is its description of where verification ends, not the classification itself.

## Later Review Addendum

Reviewing the old investigation records confirms that the issue name and call name had led readers to that file. It does not confirm that the file itself is where the embedded plugin implementation belongs, or that its contents alone can establish the loading result. Image names, template references, and the final loadable contents may be determined jointly by adjacent locations; the old record did not preserve those relationships individually.

The May wording "sole entry point" is therefore changed to "first verification entry point." This change does not reverse the original decision: R29 retains the embedded plugin classification, and a single review does not justify inventing a separate maintenance track. Only the stopping condition for verification changes: after reading the image-side declarations, they cannot be taken directly as proof that the release artifact already contains the plugin.

The diagram below preserves only this page's old reading order. It is not an implementation relationship diagram; the final state means an actual check is required, and no conclusion can be inferred automatically from the preceding state.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Embedded_plugin_history
  Embedded_plugin_history --> Image_side_reading_entry_point: Earlier investigation
  Image_side_reading_entry_point --> Release_verification: Requires a separate check
```

## Division of Responsibility with Actual Verification

KONE-211 makes the follow-up check more specific: use the release command that maintainers use in their day-to-day work to check this item, and record the failure stage separately from downloadable artifacts. The card is suited to capturing material from an actual run; this page preserves the earlier classification decision, and the existence of the card cannot substitute for that check.

This also explains why the image-side reading record cannot be retroactively marked "plugin verified." If the actual check stops at a failure stage, record where it stopped; if it leaves a downloadable artifact, that artifact should provide the corresponding confirmation. The old decision did not preserve the result of that run, and this addendum should not invent a result for it.

## Record-Keeping Conclusions That Still Stand

1. Cilium 1.15.2 will continue to be recorded as an embedded plugin item for R29, with no separate external integration record.
2. `pkg/templates/images/images.go` can still serve as the starting point for the old investigation, but is no longer treated as sufficient proof of the release contents.
3. The loading result should be confirmed by the failure-stage or artifact records from actual release verification; this old decision record does not make that determination.

The old draft did not specify which template reference to inspect first when continuing from the image side, nor did it leave a result for Cilium 1.15.2 from the actual release command. Once someone finds the relevant material via KONE-211, they can append the result; until then, the first draft's claim that "following this file is enough to confirm it" should be read as an earlier assessment that has been corrected.

# VCD CSI expansion proposal

R29 Treat the VCD CSI 1.6.0 resizer as a separate trial, rather than combining it with the remaining CSI updates. There isn't enough evidence to attribute the issue to the version itself, the configuration entry point, or a particular caller. Keep that boundary in place to avoid changing the entire storage chain in a rush to release.

The initial approach is to find the last working set of artifacts and compare the resizer-related jobs and pinned versions item by item. If an item has no clear change, don't rewrite it for this trial. This keeps the diff small, so even if we need to roll back later, we can return to the original artifact combination.

There are two opposing approaches: update all related jobs together, or keep pinning the old versions. The former would expand the scope to usage patterns we haven't investigated; the latter would obscure the parts of R29 that actually need adjustment. Don't choose either yet; use the diff results to decide which single item to change.

Start tracing back from `pkg/cmd/config.go`. The `cmd` package and adjacent imports are visible here, making it a sufficient starting point on the configuration side. The resizer's actual ownership and the conditions that trigger the failure still need to be confirmed at the reference sites.

Rollback condition: if maintaining the result requires changing multiple unrelated jobs at once, stop this trial and restore the last working set of artifacts. Don't make the temporary combination the default path.

Still needed: a minimal reproduction for the specific usage pattern; whether the pinned version is the only change; whether the configuration entry point played a part in the selection.

versions.body:
# VCD CSI Expansion Plan

The first draft focused on "avoiding wholesale updates." That direction still stands, but it treated the old artifact as an approximate baseline without defining the scope clearly enough. The counterexample found during review does not show that all VCD CSI usage patterns are abnormal. Rather, one point remains unconfirmed in a specific usage pattern of the VCD CSI 1.6.0 resizer. This round therefore no longer considers replacing the entire set of CSI components at once. It only considers how to keep changes to R29 distinguishable.

KONE-212 can serve as the navigation entry point for this work. The card's requirement is narrow too: check "VCD CSI 1.6.0 resizer" against the last usable artifact, and update only jobs or pinned versions that have actually changed. "Update only" does not mean assuming the old versions are problem-free. It means refusing to add items outside this comparison to the release diff along the way.

## Withdraw an overly broad assumption first

The first draft listed "update all related jobs together" as a possible quick fix. We are not adopting that option. It would reduce the apparent differences between version combinations, but it would also make it impossible to attribute subsequent results to the resizer, a job, or a pinned version. For R29, what is missing is not a larger change set, but a change set that explains where the differences come from.

The opposite approach is to keep the last usable artifact unchanged as a whole. That cannot be the conclusion either. If the specific usage pattern does depend on a changed job or pinned version, holding the whole artifact unchanged would only hide the change; it would not establish that the resizer can still be used as before. In this discussion, the old artifact is therefore the comparison reference and rollback target, not a permanent option.

Only one approach remains: start from the last usable artifact and first list the jobs and pinned versions adjacent to that usage pattern. An item enters the R29 combination only if the comparison can identify a change in it. Items without evidence of a change stay as they were. The cost of this approach is that review must accept blanks marked "not yet known," rather than filling them with a seemingly complete set of upgrades.

## What this comparison needs to answer

The comparison proceeds through three smaller questions, rather than asking "has the artifact been updated?":

- Does this specific usage pattern show differences only on the resizer side;
- Is a given job actually part of this difference, rather than neighboring content in the same artifact;
- After a pinned version changes, can the results still be mapped item by item to the last usable artifact.

If the first question has no answer, that does not justify relabeling the issue as a general VCD CSI anomaly. If the second has no answer, the job cannot be added to the update list. If the third has no answer, the pinned-version change cannot be treated as a completed compatibility determination. These are gaps at different levels; a single "update succeeded" cannot stand in for all of them.

After a design comparison during review, we retained these three questions and the direction of narrowly scoped updates. That comparison did not turn the one unconfirmed usage pattern into an established conclusion. This page therefore records neither a complete compatibility determination nor a broader claim of full support for VCD CSI 1.6.0.

## Where to check on the configuration side

`pkg/cmd/config.go` remains the configuration-side entry point for this round. What is visible in the file is `package cmd` and the import block. This can help trace outward from the area around command configuration, but this location alone cannot establish where the resizer implementation belongs. What needs tracing is the references and version selections actually encountered in the comparison, not treating this filename as the cause of the problem.

This arrangement also has a practical benefit: if a change later turns out to come from the configuration path, the record can be supplemented on the configuration side. If the change belongs only to a job or pinned version, mentioning the entry-point file will not cause it to be misrecorded as a command-layer change. The available material does not support a more specific attribution, so we will not invent one.

## Adoption and rollback

The proposed release combination should meet two requirements: each change from the last usable artifact can be explained, and only jobs or pinned versions that have actually changed are updated. This does not require closing out every possible VCD CSI usage pattern in the same round. The one unconfirmed point should remain open.

The rollback triggers are narrowed accordingly: if keeping this specific usage pattern passing requires changing multiple jobs without supporting comparison evidence, or if the relationship between a pinned version and the results cannot be explained, roll back to the last usable artifact. Rollback does not mark the unconfirmed item as resolved; it stops the temporary combination from being advanced to R29.

The earlier statement that "keeping the old artifact fixed is enough" no longer applies, because it mistook the comparison reference for the conclusion. The earlier statement that "all related jobs should be updated together" no longer applies either, because it would erase the differences this trial needs to preserve. Both assessments remain in the record so that later readers can see why this round accepts only narrower changes.

Still open: the anomaly in that one specific usage pattern of the VCD CSI 1.6.0 resizer has not been confirmed; a minimal reproduction is not included on this page; and the relationship between the configuration-side entry point and the actual version selection has not been established as causal. KONE-212 will continue to carry this investigation until the scope of the anomaly, the items that actually changed, and the rollback boundaries can each be documented clearly.

# Node hostname preflight troubleshooting tree

R29's Node hostname Preflight returned different results after an upgrade than it had before. Treat it first as a regression in the preflight check itself; don't immediately frame the investigation around node reconciliation, control-plane role labels, or cloud-provider defaulting.

Keep three things during the investigation: the context that triggered the preflight check, the name seen in the node object, and the raw message from the preflight check. Identical names don't mean identical inputs; in particular, don't just substitute a node name already present in the cluster for the hostname received by that preflight run.

```text
Unexpected preflight result
├─ Reproducible with the same input
│  └─ Compare this run's hostname with the node name, and keep the raw message
├─ Occurs only after an upgrade
│  └─ First record how nodes were prepared before and after the upgrade
└─ Not consistently reproducible
   └─ Don't change the preflight rules based on this; leave it for review first
```

Older records point the issue name and call name to `pkg/scripts/node.go`. Start by checking around that file, then decide whether to trace further back to the caller. If only the symptom can be confirmed, record it as unresolved; don't document a temporary workaround as a recovery procedure.

versions.body:
# Node hostname pre-check troubleshooting tree

The easiest place for this investigation to go off track is conflating "what the node was later called in the cluster" with "what hostname the pre-check received at the time." R29 After an upgrade, people may first see a regression in the pre-check result, and only later see clues left by the node object, node reconciliation, or environment preparation. When the order is reversed, the investigation quickly lands on a conclusion that looks reasonable but does not explain the original message.

The starting point here is always the pre-check anomaly itself. Once you receive the report, first preserve the original message from that run; do not rewrite it as "the node name is wrong" or "the node is not registered." Then record which node preparation stage the pre-check occurred in, whether that node came through the upgrade path, and the hostname visible at the time. If any one of these details is missing, fill in the record first; do not use another node's successful result as a substitute.

```text
Node hostname Preflight Anomaly
|
+-- Original message is still available, and the node that triggered the pre-check is known
|   |
|   +-- The same message appears again on the same node
|   |   |
|   |   +-- hostname differs from the name shown by the node object
|   |   |   `-- Record the two values separately first; continue checking where the pre-check obtains its value
|   |   |
|   |   `-- They are the same
|   |       `-- Do not rule out the pre-check based on this; check differences in node preparation before and after the upgrade
|   |
|   `-- It does not appear again on rerun
|       `-- Preserve the first message and the environment changes; do not modify the rules or announce recovery
|
+-- The original message is incomplete, or the node cannot be identified
|   `-- Stop before reproduction: fill in the node, preparation stage, and message before continuing
|
`-- Only a secondhand description of a "regression after upgrade" is available
    `-- Confirm the actual scope first; the hostname source cannot be inferred from the description
```

## First distinguish the two names you see

The investigation record should write the hostname and the name shown by the node object separately. The former is the object the pre-check is meant to evaluate; the latter is a visible result in the cluster state. If the two happen to match, that only means there is no obvious difference this time; it does not imply that the pre-check definitely read the value from the node object. Conversely, a difference between them is not yet the root cause: the inputs to the node preparation stage may differ, or the upgrade process may have caused the two observation points to fall at different times.

Therefore, do not write only "the names match" or "the names do not match" in the report. At minimum, fill in the facts from the following three statements separately:

- Which node triggered the pre-check;
- What hostname was captured at the time;
- What name was seen from the node object.

If the third item is temporarily unavailable, you can still continue checking the pre-check entry point; do not guess a node name just to make the record complete. If the first item cannot be determined, you should not continue comparing names. That kind of issue may look like a hostname regression, but in practice it can only be classified as a failure report without node context.

## From the symptom to the code entry point

The existing old record leads from the issue name and call name to `pkg/scripts/node.go`. This review can confirm that the file belongs to the `scripts` package and that the file header contains the following directly visible structure:

```go
package scripts

import (
```

This is sufficient as a point to trace back from, but it is not a substitute for checking references. After opening the file, first search for declarations and call sites adjacent to node, hostname, and the pre-check message; while reviewing them, prioritize one narrow question: does this location handle hostname directly, or does it merely delegate node-related work elsewhere? Do not assume it is the pre-check implementation just because the filename contains node.

If you find a location near that file that directly handles hostname, the next step is to compare it with the hostname recorded at the time of failure. Compare the source of the value and the timing of its handling, not merely whether the variable or function names look similar. If you find only forwarding, assembly, or a call entry, state that clearly and continue along the actual call relationship; do not repeatedly modify the current file to validate a guess.

If no adjacent location can be found in the file, that does not mean the old record is invalid. Simply retain the status "entered `pkg/scripts/node.go` from the issue name and call name; whether it is a direct handling point has not yet been confirmed." This conclusion is more useful than expanding the path into a complete implementation chain, because a later review can restart from the same location.

## First determine whether this is an upgrade boundary

"Regression in the result after upgrade" is the entry point for this issue, not an attribution that has already been completed. Before starting the comparison, first separate nodes in the upgrade path from nodes not in the upgrade path. Do not mix different node preparation methods into one comparison table; otherwise, a single difference may be misread as a version difference.

For nodes in the upgrade path, ask in sequence: did the anomaly appear as soon as the pre-check ran, or was it only noticed after the node had already been created; did all nodes of the same type show it; were the original messages left behind the same? The first question distinguishes the pre-check scene from a later state, the second limits the scope, and the third prevents different anomalies from being put into the same issue.

If only one node shows the issue, do not immediately call it a general regression. First save that node's hostname, node object name, and preparation stage separately. Only when multiple nodes produce the same type of message under comparable conditions is it worth expanding the investigation to the common upgrade path. "Comparable" does not need to be defined as a large matrix first; at minimum, do not treat an upgraded node and a node that has never gone through that path as the same body of evidence.

If the anomaly was discovered only after the upgrade, but no one preserved the message from when the pre-check occurred, do not fabricate a failure message. You can continue checking the node state and code entry point, but the conclusion should stop at "hostname pre-check issue observed after the upgrade." It cannot directly become "the upgrade changed the hostname."

## Handling order while the anomaly message is still available

When the original message exists, first perform a check that does not change the node configuration. Read the hostname recorded at the time, read the name in the node object, confirm that they came from the same node, and then check whether the pre-check entry point has a corresponding value retrieval or comparison nearby. This order is intentionally slower: it prevents changing the node first and losing the difference afterward.

In the branch where the two values differ, do not immediately modify the node name. First confirm whether the hostname seen by the pre-check came from the node preparation process. If it came from the preparation process, changing the node object in the cluster may not change the next pre-check; if it came from a later state, only then is it necessary to continue checking when the state changed. Before the source is confirmed, any operation to "align the names" is only a probe and cannot be written into the recovery steps.

In the branch where the two values match, do not simply assign the issue to another module either. You still need to confirm whether the pre-check comparison is limited to string equality and whether the failure message is emitted by an adjacent condition. Here, return to the actual call relationship around `pkg/scripts/node.go`. If you can locate the comparison point, record the values before and after the comparison; if you can locate only the entry point, record the entry point and the unconfirmed items, without packaging a guess as a fix.

When both the original message and the current node state are available but cannot be matched to the same node, stop first. A common mistake is to use a node added or reconciled later to explain an old message. You may save the two records side by side at this point, but do not continue inferring the root cause from the name difference. You first need to regain a pre-check scene that can be matched to the node.

## What not to do when reproduction is unstable

Failure to reproduce consistently does not mean the anomaly has disappeared. It only means that the same phenomenon was not obtained again under the current conditions. The most valuable action at this point is to preserve the original message from the first failure, the triggering node, and the upgrade context, then record a later attempt in which it did not appear. The fact that the two results differ is itself a difference that needs explanation.

Do not directly tighten or loosen the hostname pre-check in this branch. Changing the rules will remove the baseline for later comparisons and obscure the original regression. Also, do not treat a pass after rerunning once as completed recovery; that successful run may have used a different node, a different preparation stage, or may simply not have hit the same conditions again.

If you must continue with other work, record a clear stopping point: an anomaly that has not been reproduced is not a basis for modifying the pre-check logic. If you encounter the same type of message later, first fill in the three items listed at the beginning of this page, then decide whether to merge the two events. This will not resolve the first failure, but it will prevent a broad "intermittent" label from covering it.

## Adjacent issues not to mix in

Node hostname Preflight, node reconciliation, Control Plane role label Reconciliation, and nil host label Initialization may all appear in the same investigation, but they are not the same object. When a node name looks abnormal, it is easy to check labels first; when an upgrade scenario appears, it is also easy to attribute the issue to defaulting. Unless the original message or a code reference clearly connects them, do not first write these objects into the same attribution.

Likewise, cloud provider defaulting, the scheduling order of external CCM, and differences in embedded manifest rendering may all affect the node's final state, but they cannot replace the on-site record of the hostname pre-check. They should become the next branch only when the local comparison has already shown that the hostname's source or timing is related to them. Otherwise, the record becomes very difficult to unwind: every adjacent module has been suspected, while the actual pre-check input was never preserved.

This is also why this page does not begin with "check all upgrade components first." A pre-check failure has its own minimum scene. Restore that minimum scene first, then connect the related issues one by one; the investigation will be much shorter.

## Addendum to this review

KONE-213 confirmed the issue scope as a post-upgrade result regression for Node hostname Preflight, and processing then began. The review did not add a newly verified implementation attribution; what it actually added was the path from the card back to the code entry point, along with a recording method that no longer conflates hostname with the node object name.

The card is used to return to the context of this regression: KONE-213. The item in the card that still needs verification remains valid: the maintainer of the corresponding module needs to confirm the behavior in the current version and point out an entry point for further checking. The entry point that can already be provided here is `pkg/scripts/node.go`, but whether it is a direct handling point still needs to be confirmed through that revision's reference relationships.

The current handling can be divided into two types of handoff. The first preserves the specific failed node, hostname, and original message, and the person taking over continues checking the declarations and call sites near the file; the second contains only a description of the regression after the upgrade, and the person taking over first fills in the pre-check scene instead of starting to change the rules. Neither handoff should carry an assumption such as "the name mismatch is the cause."

## Record format

For each new case, a short record is enough; there is no need to write another long narrative:

```text
Node:
hostname:
Node object name:
Original pre-check message:
Stage of occurrence:
On upgrade path:
Retry attempt:
Code entry verification:
Not yet confirmed:
```

For "Retry attempt," write only the actual result obtained, such as whether the message still appears and whether it can still be matched to the same node; do not fill in the expected result. For "Code entry verification," record the specific file and the locations already reviewed. If the entry point has not yet been expanded, retain `pkg/scripts/node.go`; do not fill in an unverified function name just to make the table look complete.

Only when the pre-check message, hostname, and node object name can be matched to the same node, and the code location can also show where the value retrieval or comparison occurs, may this case be advanced from a "regression report" to a concrete cause. Until then, the recovery actions on this page are limited to preserving the scene, narrowing the scope, and stopping changes that lack a basis.

# CSI Migration Gate Check Procedure

This record was retained alongside the compatibility checks for R29. Its original wording was straightforward: the old investigation notes listed "CSI migration completion gate" alongside a call name, then marked `pkg/apis/kubeone/helpers.go` as the first file to open. Anyone taking over can indeed start here, without first having to guess which layer of the full code tree contains those names.

The problem with the early notes was not choosing the wrong entry point, but making "found the entry point" sound almost like "found the completion check." What is visible in that file is `package kubeone` and the nearby direct dependencies. It is useful for local navigation, but cannot, on its own, show that a particular compatibility caller has already gone through the gate. The old record was not deleted, because historical lookups still start with this set of names; but its "central location" wording should be treated only as a working assumption made at the time.

## Retained Original Procedure

The original migration sequence was:

1. Start with the gate name and the old call name to get to `pkg/apis/kubeone/helpers.go`.
2. Pin the revision selected for that review, and check only the references that can be found in that revision.
3. List the call names before and after the change side by side. The old notes treated an unchanged name as an unchanged path.
4. If there is a mismatch, return to the original call name and reference location, and wait for the next check.

Step 3 later proved insufficient. Keeping the name only shows that the navigation term is still there; it does not prove that the same compatibility check is still being called. This change in wording does not require turning the old notes into a full code walkthrough; their value was always in recording where the search began at the time and where to fall back to midway through.

# R29 Control Plane Label Decision Record

This record did not start with a complete design. Someone followed the issue name "Control Plane role label Reconciliation" to `pkg/tasks/nodes.go`, then quickly linked the file path to ownership of the behavior. The decision for R29 initially stayed within a narrower scope: retain the existing call, find a genuinely reachable test or example path, then determine whether the gap occurs before entering the task or within reconciliation itself. This order was retained after review.

## The decision recorded for now

The decision is: do not use the requirements history of R29 as a reason to move, split, or delete the existing Control Plane role label Reconciliation call. There is currently no evidence supporting a separate set of replacement rules, nor any evidence that external steps can replace this existing behavior. If later changes alter the label results, the discussion must be reopened with new evidence about paths or results; ownership judgments cannot be changed solely on the basis of the directory containing the file.

The practical approach on the quality side was also settled. Use an existing test or example as the triggering entry point, and record the scenario it describes, whether it actually reaches the reconciliation call, and the user paths it does not cover. What needs to be confirmed here is the path, not merely the presence of nodes or labels in a test name. An assertion whose setup starts with a downstream object can establish a local result, but cannot by itself show that the user entry point passed through the task-side call.

This decision does not require creating a new test file, nor does it assign all label semantics to a single task function. Existing tests and existing examples can both serve as entry points; the difference is what each can prove: the former may be better suited to stable regression testing, while the latter may be closer to user configurations. The record should preserve this distinction, rather than describing a single result check as coverage of the entire path.

## The strong claim in the initial draft

The initial draft described `pkg/tasks/nodes.go` as the only location for reconciliation. This judgment remains in the history as the working assumption at the time, but it is no longer treated as certain in the current decision. The earlier investigation did lead from the issue name and call name to this file; `package tasks` and `import (` can also be seen in the file header. This information is enough to help later readers reopen the task-side code, but it does not establish that inputs are constructed here, defaults are determined here, or all control plane node paths pass through here.

The choice not to move it at that point was not based on proof that the file could not be changed. The real reason was that the questions "is the existing call triggered by a user path" and "should the reconciliation code be refactored" had not yet been separated. Extracting a new entry point first would change directories, calls, and coverage at the same time; even if test results changed afterward, it would be difficult to tell whether this reflected a gap in the original path or a behavioral difference introduced by the migration. Retaining the call and gathering path evidence first was therefore a deliberate choice to limit the scope of impact.

The initial draft also tended to treat "add a label-result assertion" as the smallest fix. After review, this can still be part of regression testing, but it cannot close this item on its own. A result assertion answers what the constructed object ultimately looks like, while a trigger record answers which user configuration, test, or example brought execution to the reconciliation location. The two are related, but they are not the same thing.

## Approaches that were compared

### Extract a standalone reconciliation layer

The advantage of this approach is that the naming and directory layout might be easier to understand. Concentrating all role label logic in one location would save a few steps during later investigation. However, it requires knowing the full context of the existing call first, and confirming that all types of input still arrive at the same time after migration. If the current file is only one part of the surrounding task-side code, extracting it prematurely would hide the actual entry point; if there are callers that have not yet been discovered, the new layer would not necessarily cover them automatically either.

This approach is therefore not being adopted for now, rather than being rejected permanently. A standalone reconciliation layer will have a new basis for evaluation only when trigger records show repeated reconciliation across multiple independent paths, or show that `nodes.go` is merely a forwarding entry point. At that point, specific paths must be used to compare inputs and results before and after migration; similar filenames alone cannot justify a split.

### Only add label-result assertions

This approach involves the smallest change and can quickly pin down the output of a particular construction scenario. Its problem is also clear: a test may start from an object downstream of the task, so a passing assertion does not mean that the real entry point passed through Control Plane role label Reconciliation; conversely, an example may pass through the entry point without checking the label results. Both kinds of record are worth retaining, but each must state the limited portion it confirms.

Result assertions can therefore be added alongside existing tests or examples, but they do not replace records of triggering paths. R29 first needs to know whether a visible entry point can lead to the call, before deciding whether deeper behavioral assertions are needed. If a user configuration has no corresponding test or example, record that gap rather than masking it with a successful result from a neighboring scenario.

### Keep using the existing call, establish the entry point first

This is the approach currently being adopted. It does not require assuming code ownership in advance, nor does it require designing a new interface before user inputs have been clarified. Specifically, select an existing test or example that can be inspected, and confirm whether it enters Control Plane role label Reconciliation; then record covered scenarios separately from uncovered user paths. If this verification overturns the original judgment about the entry point, the findings themselves become evidence for the next decision.

The cost is that there will not be a neat, unified structural diagram in the short term. The record may add only a note about "what this example triggered and what it did not trigger", leaving several questions unanswered. But this is more reliable than using a directory reorganization to create a sense of completion. The current goal is not to prove that all possible inputs are covered, but to let the next discussion begin with an identifiable path.

## Location and boundaries

`pkg/tasks/nodes.go` remains the starting point for tracing the code for this item. When tracing it, first look at the file's task-side location under `package tasks`, then follow its direct dependencies to confirm the call context; seeing `import (` only establishes that the file has a set of dependencies, not that those dependencies form the complete label-generation chain. The navigation relationships in the earlier investigation record can be retained because they explain why the investigation starts here, but navigation should not be presented as proof of implementation ownership.

This decision covers only retaining Control Plane role label Reconciliation and recording its triggering and coverage. It does not prescribe the keys and values of all node labels, does not prescribe generation order, and does not draw conclusions about the neighboring interface initialization issue. nil host label Initialization has a separate record at DOC-26; the two efforts may intersect during verification, but the input state of one cannot currently be treated directly as the cause of the other.

The boundary between the task side and the quality side is likewise kept to the minimum supported by the evidence. The task side needs to be able to describe the state actually received around the existing call; the quality side needs to retain records of whether a test or example reaches that call. Both sides can identify uncovered paths, but one side keeping entry-point records does not imply that the other owns all label semantics. Integration scenarios need to use this record to determine whether regression testing was triggered, not as a basis for taking over rule definition.

## How to review a record

An adequate trigger record must include at least the local scenario, the entry-point type, and whether the call was reached. The scenario should state whether it targets control plane nodes; the entry-point type should specify an existing test or an existing example; the outcome should state whether execution actually passed through reconciliation, only the final object was checked, or this remains unconfirmed. These three cannot be replaced with a single "pass".

If a test name includes role label but its setup starts with a downstream object, record it as a result check rather than a path trigger. If an example enters the task-side call without checking the final labels, it can be recorded as trigger confirmation, but do not describe it as complete regression coverage. This distinction may make the records look less tidy, but it prevents entry-point coverage and output coverage from being conflated into a single judgment.

There is no need to infer a complete set of uncovered user paths from the issue name. Once it is known that a configuration or example does not reach the existing call, record that fact and preserve its distinction from the covered scenarios. What remains unknown is whether an entry point, an input, or an assertion is missing; do not settle on a cause before obtaining the corresponding evidence.

## Decision state transitions

The current choice can be condensed into the following state relationships. They describe the workflow for this item, not a new implementation structure:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ExistingCall
    ExistingCall --> TriggerRecord: Retain reconciliation
    TriggerRecord --> CoverageConfirmed: Test or example actually reaches the call
    TriggerRecord --> PathPendingCoverage: Not yet covered
    PathPendingCoverage --> Reassessment: Obtain evidence for a specific path
    Reassessment --> ExistingCall: No migration for now
    Reassessment --> IndependentReconciliationLayer: Duplicate entry points found
```

The "independent reconciliation layer" in the diagram is a follow-up option that was compared, not a new module that R29 has already decided to introduce; "coverage confirmed" likewise means only that one entry-point verification is complete, not that all user scenarios are covered. If subsequent records do not show duplicate entry points, continue working through the existing call; do not add new implementation conclusions merely to fill out the state diagram.

## Matters that remain open

There is still no explicitly named existing test or example that can serve as a stable triggering entry point for Control Plane role label Reconciliation. The input used and whether execution reached the call must be documented after actual verification. This decision also cannot supply the uncovered user paths; they should be recorded one by one as entry points are verified, rather than starting with a seemingly complete set.

If the review finds similar entry points beyond `nodes.go`, the next record should compare their actual relationships before deciding whether extracting a standalone layer is worthwhile. Without such evidence, maintain this decision: retain the existing call, confirm the path with an identifiable test or example, and clearly record label-result checks and entry-point coverage separately.

# nil host label adjustment proposal

This review originally started from `pkg/apis/kubeone/types.go`. At the time, the issue was described as "the host label needs to be initialized when it is nil," so attention naturally focused on the area around the API object. The initial draft leaned toward creating an empty map before role-label writes for the object and treating nil checks scattered across call sites as a second-best option.

That judgment is retained here because it explains why the subsequent review did not directly carry the initial draft forward. The path is indeed suitable for checking the declaration and label-related fields; it does not, by itself, establish who owns the defaulting step. Treating the location of the object definition as the owner of initialization was a working assumption made to move the review forward, not a confirmed implementation relationship.

## Branches left by the initial draft

The two directions listed at the time are still useful for reference; they should simply be compared based on the semantics they affect.

**Initialize at the common entry point.** If all hosts that need role labels pass through the same entry point, convert nil labels to an empty map there, allowing Fang Ke to handle only the label contents. The benefit of this approach is that the rule is centralized, and it prevents different write points from independently deciding what nil means during the same reconciliation. The cost is that the entry point must actually cover all relevant objects; if it also serves paths that do not write role labels, eager allocation changes the object's state from "labels not provided" to "empty labels provided."

**Initialize at the write point.** Create the map only before writing role labels. This keeps the scope closer to the actual action and does not require all preceding hosts to share a defaulting stage. The cost is that every write point must be found; if one branch is missed, nil will still appear later. The initial draft described this option too conservatively, as if it only led to duplicate code. On review, it is instead a candidate worth retaining when the caller's semantics are unclear.

**Reject or skip nil.** This was not presented as the recommended option, but it cannot be removed from the review record. If nil is deliberately retained by the caller, silently creating an empty map masks invalid input; if role labels are not the object's responsibility, skipping the write may better fit the original boundary. The available material does not provide enough evidence to choose this branch, so it is a branch to reassess if the first two options are withdrawn, not new behavior to add immediately.

## Later review

The checks left by KONE-217 did not require changing the declaration directly. They required finding a caller that still uses "nil host label Initialization" and verifying its actual version, entry point, and current result. This narrows the review to one real call chain: first confirm where nil comes from, then determine where it first becomes a writable label collection, and only then decide whether initialization should be moved up to the common entry point.

The review can record three inputs, but they should not be combined: no labels, an empty map, and existing labels. The first two may produce the same result on some write paths, but that does not establish that they are always equivalent in serialization, defaulting, or caller checks. The third input is used to confirm that initialization does not overwrite content already supplied by the caller. What is needed here is one comparison along the call chain, not a set of abstract interface assertions.

`pkg/apis/kubeone/types.go` continues to serve as the lookup entry point: first check whether the declaration permits nil, then follow the actual caller to confirm the point adjacent to the label write. If the review finds that initialization has already been performed by the caller, the original "initialize at the common entry point" recommendation should be marked as not applicable. If multiple callers all pass nil directly into the same role-reconciliation point, reinstate that recommendation and limit initialization to the point before it.

## Review stopping point

Before finding the caller, do not add defaulting based solely on the object definition. That would turn a single nil guard into a API state change and make later readers think that all hosts need labels. Conversely, if the caller found has already explicitly allocated a map before entering role reconciliation, this proposal has no remaining changes and should only be retained as a record of the earlier judgment.

If multiple entry points are found and they handle nil differently, do not use initialization in one place to flatten those differences. First mark separately which entry points write role labels and which only pass the host through; the common-entry approach is valid only when nil has the same semantics on these paths.

The decision remains open. The initial direction can be used to prepare a localized diff, but it cannot be treated as a conclusion to add defaulting before release. Until the caller check required by KONE-217 is complete, the withdrawal criteria remain unchanged: the caller uses nil as a meaningful state, or the initialization point is not on the common path for role-label writes.
