## At the boundary

- [ ] Stop the ongoing cleanup when you read "rollback boundary." Stopping does not mean rollback succeeded; it only prevents further changes beyond the boundary.
- [ ] When recovery is needed, do not write recovery steps on the fly in the checklist's blank spaces. There is no record of the recovery actions having worked end to end in the shared environment, and the old version did not provide a reusable sequence either.
- [ ] Stop if the `scenario generator` does not appear. When it is absent, the last visible result cannot serve as a substitute.
- [ ] Have the person originally responsible review the exit actions. If there is no reply, retain "no reply" and where work stopped; do not classify waiting as completion.
- [ ] After the checks are complete, the relevant owner must still sign off separately on whether the release succeeded. Checking off the list only indicates that these limited checks were carried out.

Do not delete results already recorded before "rollback boundary" appeared. If there are further attempts after the boundary, do not overwrite the original last result; they belong to another action and must not be backfilled as the end of the old window. The old checklist only required stopping cleanup and did not provide a sequence for recovery actions, so "already stopped" does not imply "already recovered."

An old sequence that is easy to misuse is kept here: look at the result first, then go back and look at the action. It used to make closeout easier, but can lead to "the last result" being misread as "the last action has completed." Subsequent records should clearly state the exit actions first, then attach the result; this page does not backfill the missing parts of old windows or rewrite old records as if they had followed the new sequence.

## Card records added alongside the checklist later

KONEA-003 has a record of `interface_reviewed` and was subsequently marked `work_started (To Do → In Progress)`. These two items show that an interface review and the start of work were recorded, but they are not exit actions and cannot substitute for the owner's release sign-off. In particular, "start work" only indicates that a state change occurred; it must not be moved into the window-close field as the last result.

The description on the same card requires contacting the person originally responsible before the exit actions are due; if there is no reply, close out using the existing exit actions. This can explain why the checklist contains "no reply" and a stopping point, but it does not turn waiting into completion. Review by the person originally responsible is still a hold point, not a step that can be replaced by an adjacent status.

KONEA-008 has one instance of `baseline_recorded` recorded. The note says, "The person on duty replied to the previous entry, not this card." This record therefore cannot be appended to the last result for this window. The old version tended to treat adjacent records as supporting evidence; this time it is kept only as a counterexample: if a card reply does not explicitly apply to the current item, do not use it to fill in the exit checklist.

Another requirement in KONEA-008 is to check both the current entry point and the original current revision; if both are missing, leave the status unknown. Here, unknown applies only to that card's collection status; it cannot be used to assert that the exit actions succeeded, failed, or no longer need review. It also cannot make up for the missing recovery records in the checklist.

Related entry points can be found through KONEA-003 and KONEA-008, but cards do not replace the item-by-item hold points in the checklist. If the result is empty, the actions have not been reviewed, or the rollback boundary has already appeared, the window remains stopped at the current record. Release sign-off continues to be handled separately by the relevant owner.

Recovery actions are still the missing piece. The old page only required that the environment not be cleaned up and left no result from a completed recovery; this is also why it is still retained, but should not be treated as the release rules in effect.

# Release Automation Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

When release automation gets stuck, first check whether the incident record is still available, rather than first asking whether this run can be rerun successfully. The record must retain at least the original input, version identifier, and first visible result; a green result added later only shows that a later run passed and cannot replace the first result.

```text
Original record available?
├─ No
│  └─ Collect it; do not enter root-cause discussion
└─ Yes
   ├─ Kustomization does not appear
   │  └─ Stop at the rendering entry point; retain the content before and after the scenario generator
   └─ Kustomization appears
      ├─ Matches a normal sample from the compatibility window
      │  └─ Check the current entry point or environment; if it remains within the project, the on-duty person handles it
      └─ The first difference is a mismatch
         ├─ It is a version identifier or version matrix
         │  └─ Clearly identify the objects, then hand off to whoever can confirm the matrix
         ├─ Requires changing the test fixture
         │  └─ Hand off to someone who can modify the fixture
         └─ Requires a permission change or an exit action
            └─ Stop with the corresponding owner
```

### Disambiguate objects with the same name first

KONEB-009 notes that the same-named apis-release-automation object is missing a version identifier. When you encounter descriptions like "the same release is still queued," first separate the object under review from the old object, then compare them. Directory names, task titles, and statuses displayed later are not sufficient substitutes for a version identifier.

If the first difference is in the version, record both sides' versions and stop at the version matrix. Do not switch to another version before checking the result, and do not treat "most recent success" as showing that the original version is normal. When the previous owner is not part of this cycle, the current on-duty person takes over this diagnostic step; the on-duty person is responsible only for documenting the object and the difference clearly and does not replace the matrix maintainer in making the compatibility judgment.

### No artifact at the rendering entry point

When Kustomization does not appear after the scenario generator, first retain the input before the generator and the first result after the generator. At this point, do not switch to checking the final artifact or explain the stall using average elapsed time. The absence of Kustomization only warrants stopping the investigation at the rendering entry point.

If Kustomization has appeared, compare it against a normal sample from the same compatibility window. First check whether the entry point and environment differ; continue to version comparison only if they are the same. If the environment or entry-point difference is still internal to apis · Release Automation, the current on-duty person continues; if it requires crossing an interface that has already been agreed on, document the handoff point before handing it off.

### Fixtures and old tasks

The reason for the handoff in KONEB-012 is that the testing phase needs someone who can modify fixtures. If troubleshooting requires adjusting a fixture to proceed, first hand the original failed sample to someone with permission to make that change; do not make the party without modification authority rerun it repeatedly. If, at the end of the window, the result still has not been updated and the old task is still occupying its place, do not overwrite it with a new task; mark the old assessment and append the new result beside it.

Once, a retry was started too early, and the original run context was overwritten by a later green result. Change this to: save the first failed sample and the environment differences before deciding whether to retry. A retry may only be used to validate a hypothesis that has already been written down; it is not a way to capture the original run conditions.

# Release Automation Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

When release automation is reported as "stuck", first anchor the investigation at the current entry point. Here, "stuck" may mean that the queue is not progressing, rendering has not produced the expected objects, version comparison has stalled, or the process has reached a stage requiring permissions and exit actions; these must not be assigned a single shared root cause. First preserve the original input, object version, and first visible result. A later rerun that goes green can only serve as a new sample; it must not erase the evidence from the earlier run.

```text
Does the original record exist?
├─ No
│  └─ Collect the missing data and stop; do not start attributing a cause
└─ Yes
   ├─ Kustomization has not appeared
   │  └─ Stay between the scenario generator and the rendering entry point
   └─ Kustomization has appeared
      ├─ Matches a known-good sample within the compatibility window
      │  └─ Check the current entry point or environment
      └─ Mismatch at the first point of difference
         ├─ Version identifier/version matrix
         ├─ Test fixtures
         ├─ Artifact content
         └─ Permissions or exit actions
```

The purpose of the tree is not to name every type of failure, but to show the person taking over how far the preceding stage has been verified. If the preceding stage has no original record, none of the subsequent branches are valid. Do not infer intermediate steps from directory names, average durations, or the final displayed status; these may suggest where to collect data next time, but they cannot close this investigation.

## First preserve evidence that can be compared

A usable original record must bring together the input, version identifier, and first visible result from the same run. If a known-good sample is available, compare only with samples from the same compatibility window, and continue from the first difference. Change only one condition per comparison; if the entry point has changed, check the entry point first, and do not change the version at the same time.

When there is no original record, the person currently on call is responsible only for collecting the missing data. Do not simply rerun to obtain the "latest result", and do not attach a new task to an old task. After an earlier premature retry, only a green result remained, making it impossible to determine whether the failure occurred at the entry point or during rendering. From that point onward, preserve the first failing sample and environment differences; retries may only be used to test a hypothesis that has already been written down.

When the original record exists but Kustomization has not appeared, stop at the rendering entry point. Preserve both the input before the scenario generator and the first result after the generator; do not start by checking the final artifact, image resolution, or version matrix. Only after Kustomization has appeared can the comparison move on to object content, versions, or the environment. This stopping point matters: it prevents an object that has not yet been produced from being mistaken for an object with incorrect content.

## Separate releases with the same name first

KONEB-009 documented that the same-named objects for apis-release-automation lacked version identifiers. When you see "that release is still queued" or "the old task has not finished", first distinguish the object you are currently viewing from the old object. The same title, the same directory, or even the same status displayed later is not a version identifier.

When version identifiers are missing, fill in the object details before moving on to the version matrix. Do not first substitute a version that currently looks usable, and do not conclude that the original object is fine just because the most recent run succeeded. When the comparison reaches the version matrix and a compatibility decision is needed, the side that can maintain that matrix should take over; the person currently on call only needs to preserve the versions on both sides and the first difference. The same applies when the previous owner is not present in the current cycle: the person on call takes responsibility for continuing the investigation, not for making release decisions on behalf of the maintainers.

Known-good samples within the compatibility window are only used to narrow down differences. If the versions are the same but the entry points differ, stay with the entry-point and environment checks first; if the entry points are the same but the versions differ, stop at the version matrix. If the two sides cannot be matched up at all, return to the original record; do not reconstruct an imagined sequence from a summary compiled later.

## When artifact builds stall

In the path that builds `dist/kubeone`, `DEFAULT_STABLE` uses `curl` to obtain the Kubernetes version from the stable-1.29 release endpoint. When the build stage gets stuck around version selection, first check the version selection and first result preserved in the record, then decide whether to move to the version branch. Do not replace the original record with the result of a later network request, and do not attribute the problem to the endpoint without evidence.

When the version has been selected but the artifact content does not meet expectations, start by checking the resource paths that were loaded. The rendered manifests for the embedded Azure Disk addon use `csi-azuredisk/csi-azuredisk.yaml` as a loadable resource path. When the expected addon is missing from the result, first confirm whether this path was loaded in the record for that run; until that is confirmed, do not reclassify the issue as permissions or exit actions.

Handoff information at this level must specify a precise location, such as "after version selection, before resource loading" or "resources loaded, rendered content does not match". Writing only "build stuck" will make the person taking over repeat comparisons that have already been performed.

## Once the object exists, check the rendered content

After Kustomization appears, first determine whether the difference concerns ConfigMap, container configuration, or Pod structure. Do not lump these objects into a single "the manifest is wrong" issue.

Canal's ConfigMap checks start with the `data` mapping: the rendered mapping stores `canal_iface` and `canal_iface_regex`. If these two keys are absent from the rendered result, preserve the corresponding fragments of the input and result, and stop at the ConfigMap branch; do not infer that the keys must exist based on whether the container started successfully.

For the container configuration of Azure CCM and Canal, inspect the `env` list. The rendered Azure CCM and Canal containers expose the required SSL and Flannel environment variables through the Kubernetes `env` list. Differences seen here belong to the container environment variable branch and must not be mixed up with missing ConfigMap keys; the handoff record must identify which container is being compared and whether the difference occurs before or after rendering.

Start with the `spec.template` field when inspecting a workload's Pod template. If the expected object exists at the outer level but the corresponding content is missing from the template, record this location and continue checking the template; do not immediately declare that the resource was not generated. The template field and container configuration are not the same checkpoint, and they may be only one step apart in the sequence.

For volume differences, inspect the `volumes` field of PodSpec. This field declares volumes for containers to mount, including Azure CCM's host CA directory volume. The rendered Azure CCM PodSpec uses its `volumes` list to carry the host CA bundle. If the evidence only shows an abnormal mount result, without the PodSpec content from that run, stop at checking the volume declarations; do not assume that the host directory, permissions, or certificates themselves are at fault.

These checks do not require every object to be reexamined every time. Enter the corresponding branch only when the first difference has been traced to artifact content: ConfigMap goes to `data`, container variables go to `env`, template structure goes to `spec.template`, and mount declarations go to `volumes`. If there is no evidence at the preceding point, return to data collection rather than jumping to the next object.

## Fixtures, permissions, and exit actions

The reason for the handoff in KONEB-012 was that the testing stage needed someone who could modify the fixtures. If troubleshooting cannot proceed without fixture changes, first hand the original failing sample to the side authorized to modify the fixtures. The side without permission must not simulate fixture changes through repeated reruns, and must not clean up the test state before the original sample has been saved.

That card later also retained a window result that had not been updated: when the window ended, the current result had not been updated, and the old task was still in place. When you encounter this state, preserve the old assessment and append the new result alongside it; do not overwrite the old task with the new result as though both belonged to the same run. When old and new conclusions are shown side by side, first label the objects and versions corresponding to each, then decide which branch can still proceed.

A permissions issue is characterized by this: the record has already narrowed the object and difference down to a point requiring access to or modification of a resource within the project, but the current handler lacks the necessary permissions. At this point, hand the original record, object version, and tree nodes already traversed to the permissions owner. Do not describe "no permission" as a rendering failure, and do not switch to the version matrix because access cannot be obtained.

For matters requiring artifact withdrawal or changes to the user-visible contract, stop at exit actions. Resources, indexes, and existing permission issues internal to release automation can still be handled within the project; when going beyond clearly defined interfaces, changing a compatibility determination, or affecting the withdrawal window, the person currently on call does not make the final decision. In the handoff, clearly identify the objects that have been confirmed, and do not turn unverified guesses into conclusions as well.

## A few lines for the next handler

The handoff entry point is still `docs/adj-apis/runbooks/apis-release-automation-stuck-escalation-contacts.md`. Four things should be directly evident from the record: whether the original record still exists; whether the first difference lies in the entry point, rendering, versions, fixtures, artifacts, or permissions; whether the versions of same-named objects have been distinguished; and why this investigation stopped here.

KONEB-009 can be used to review how the version identifiers were sorted out, and KONEB-012 can be used to review the fixtures and old results kept side by side. DOC-34 retain only supplemental notes on temporary handoff boundaries and cannot replace the branch records here. If there is no new evidence, stop at the current node; do not supply a root cause just to complete the tree.

# Quality Signal Desk Dual-State Anomaly Postmortem

## The Two Versions Left at the Scene

The Quality Signal Desk for tasks handles failed samples, regression stratification, and unstable-signal attribution. It has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria. When the issue occurred, the current entry showed different current revisions at two points in time; the same object therefore had two states at once. Here, "two states" is not the result of combining the on-duty person, adoption status, and handling result into one field; the two records from the same entry were genuinely inconsistent.

The initial record only noted that the image parser differed from the older record. No account, version, or run id was retained for comparison; when the later retelling consisted only of screenshots, it could not explain why the other path remained normal. The original input, entry version, and recovery page were stored separately. The recovered path does not overwrite the original incident state.

The record entry for this anomaly is `docs/adj-tasks/incidents/tasks-quality-signal-board-two-states-for-one-object.md`. It is the incident-export export from the tasks · Quality Signal Board knowledge base; the body and attachments are still maintained by that project. This path only indicates where to find the original record; it does not indicate that any file is the source of the change.

## Timeline Extract

| Time point | What was observed at the scene | Action recorded |
|---|---|---|
| T+00 | `tasks-quality-signal-desk-same-object-shows-two-states` first deviated from baseline | Save the original input and entry version |
| T+07 | Compatibility window still normal | Narrow the impact scope |
| T+18 | Comparison pointed to the version matrix | Continue investigating through the corresponding entry |
| T+31 | User path recovered | Root cause remains open |

The deviation at T+00 only shows that the entry materials and the older record could not be directly aligned. It does not show whether the difference first arose in image parsing, scenario generation, precheck, or node reconciliation. Since the compatibility window at T+07 was still normal, the scope was narrowed at the time to the failed samples already seen; no declaration was made that all regression samples were affected. The version matrix at T+18 was only a direction for comparison; it cannot replace the original input. The recovery of the user path at T+31 was a recovery result, not an attribution result.

The replay of the original inputs for KONEC-003 recorded a failure classification on 2026-2-2; handling began the next day. One sample was added by KONEC-008 on 2-9. KONEC-009 then confirmed that their own incident timeline should be retained; the daily report would include only a link and would not fold this incident into another daily-report narrative. These records respectively filled in the replay, sample, and incident scope; they did not fill in the change between the two revisions.

## The Misread at the Time

The first on-call handoff interpreted the status change too quickly. The public comment from KONEC-009 later reversed itself: "I just mistook the on-duty person for the adoption status; the previous line is void." That correction remains in the incident materials because it shows that the issue was not just a display difference; it also involved a misreading of the field's meaning. It does not, in turn, prove that the cause of node reconciliation has been found.

At the time, the two relatively close explanations were that defaulting at the entry point returned the recovery path to a usable state, or that node reconciliation or the scenario generator read different content at different times. The first explanation was compatible with the recovery behavior; the second was not supported by enough counterexamples or complete records. Neither was written as the root cause in v2.

"Embedded checklist," "precheck," and "regression entry point" also appeared in separate supplemental notes. They were investigation leads, not individually confirmed locations of change. Putting these terms into a complete call chain would make the old screenshots look more complete than the evidence actually on hand, so v2 retains them only as pointers from that time.

## Impact and Recovery Assessment

The impact that can be confirmed is that the same object's entry records were inconsistent at two points in time, and this left the regression stratification of failed samples and unstable-signal attribution without a single shared reference. The compatibility window remained normal, and the user path later recovered; there is no evidence that all regression samples were affected, nor that entries for other projects changed along with it.

During recovery, the only actions were stopping retries, preserving originals, narrowing the scope, and continuing verification along the version matrix. The recovery page can show that the path became usable again; it cannot show which step changed the current revision. For branches not yet reproduced, on-call did not use the last line of green output in place of the original context.

## Records Retained

The records from KONEC-008 later stated that the basis for the handoff was "After reviewing the existing implementation, hand it off to the current module maintainer." This only shows that the review and maintenance entry points were adjusted; it does not mean responsibility attribution was complete. The two versions of the records from KONEC-009 remain stored as an independent incident timeline. Links in the daily report can provide navigation, but they cannot replace the original input, entry version, and recovery page.

Unconfirmed items include: which object changed first between the two points in time; the ordering among defaulting, node reconciliation, and image parsing; and whether regression stratification still has branches not covered by the current samples. An original comparison record containing the account, version, request context, and run id together is still missing. Without these materials, do not continue turning speculation into a conclusion.

# Quality Signal Dashboard Dual-State Anomaly Postmortem

## The original record beside the entry point

The tasks Quality Signal Dashboard page did not start out as a complete incident report. It began as a record alongside failure samples, regression stratification and attribution of unstable signals: the same object was observed at two points in time with two current revision values. The original record was not overwritten, the recovery page was saved separately, and the cause was also kept elsewhere. What was preserved this way was not a definition of two valid states, but an observation made during the incident and several subsequent explanations that did not fully align.

The project has its own schedule, maintainer and exit criteria. This boundary matters in the incident: the Quality Signal Dashboard's own samples, regression assessments and entry-point records can be kept here; whether adjacent projects experienced the same changes at the same time was not confirmed in the materials for this incident. Someone later speculated about the cause based on an adjacent service, but there was no corresponding original artifact, so the incident postmortem did not present that part as a conclusion.

The earliest material that could be identified was `docs/adj-tasks/incidents/tasks-quality-signal-board-two-states-for-one-object.md`. It came from the tasks · Quality Signal Board knowledge base's incident-export, and the main text and attachments are still maintained by that project. The page preserved the entry-point version seen at the time, rather than retaining only the page after recovery. The original record, recovery page and unconfirmed cause are each kept separately, and only then can readers see that they are not the same evidence artifact.

This path was later used repeatedly as a starting point for searches. It can help locate the incident export, but is not enough to establish which object within the entry point changed first. KONEC-003, KONEC-008, KONEC-009 appear only when navigation to replays, samples and independent incident timelines is needed; their records should not be stitched together into a new input.

## What was seen first and what was seen later

When the first deviation occurred, the on-site description was that the image resolver differed from the old record. Here "different from the old record" means only that the entry-point materials from the two occasions could not be directly aligned, not that the image resolver had already been identified as the source of the change. Initially the difference was not attributed to a release freeze, node reconciliation or any unseen caller, nor was a single green output taken as proof of recovery.

The on-call responder's first action after that was to stop further retries. Continuing to retry would produce more results from the same entry point, but would not recover the context missing when the discrepancy was first observed. Only after the original input and entry-point version were preserved, was there something that could be viewed alongside the recovery page. The recovery page shows that the path could be followed again later, but it cannot show which intervening read, generation or reconciliation changed the current revision.

The "entry point" here cannot be reduced to a page color either. At a minimum the incident simultaneously involved the old record, the current revision, what the image resolver saw and the results on the recovery page. Because these materials were not generated at the same time, using the recovery page alone to overwrite the old record would erase the differences present when the anomaly occurred; keeping only the old record would leave no way to show that the user path really did recover later.

The timeline below is the incident account retained after v2, and its time points use the relative markers from that time:

| Time point | Observation at the time | What had not been confirmed at the time |
|---|---|---|
| T+00 | `tasks-Quality Signal Dashboard-Two states appear for the same object` first deviated from the baseline | Whether the difference first arose at ingress, during parsing, or in subsequent reconciliation |
| T+07 | The compatibility window was still normal | Whether the normal window covered all failed samples |
| T+18 | The comparison pointed to the version matrix | Whether the matrix recorded triggering conditions or a snapshot of results |
| T+31 | The user path recovered | Whether the recovery action changed the current revision |

T+00 was not a finalized detection finding. It only indicated a deviation from the old records. The normal result at T+07 was used to narrow the scope, not to prove that all objects outside the failed samples were normal. T+18 gave the investigation another source of material to examine, but the version matrix did not serve as the original input in the incident. T+31 allowed the on-call response to stop, but still did not turn the preceding unknowns into knowns.

The purpose of the timeline is to separate the time of recovery from the time of root cause confirmation. The current retries could be stopped after T+31, but the path's recovery does not justify filling in the changes between T+00 and T+18 as a definite causal chain.

## Version One: A note missing timestamps

v1 contained only a very brief outline of the situation. It noted that "the image parser differed from the old records", that further retries were stopped, and that defaulting might enable recovery, while it was still unknown why node reconciliation had changed. That version had no timeline, and its body still contained an empty entry reading "Missing timestamps: ____".

That empty entry was not a date that could later be filled in casually. At the time, v1 had no account, version, request context, or run id. If more complete timestamps appear in subsequent records, they can only be treated as incident material added later, not retroactively presented as information v1 already had about the situation. v1 therefore retains its narrow perspective: it observed a difference and took action to stop retries, but did not complete the attribution.

v1 also presented "defaulting can enable recovery" as slightly more established than the evidence supported. It was a working hypothesis, not a decision. The change in node reconciliation was explicitly left as an unknown. This hypothesis was not erased during later editing, because it explains why the early responders continued to examine the recovery path; the new version also added the aspects of the hypothesis that had not been verified.

Another characteristic of v1 is that it did not treat "two states" as a state model. It simply placed the current revisions at two points in time side by side. That version did not explain how the fields were read, nor did it treat the on-call information for the person on duty as object state. The later misreading of a field cannot be projected back onto v1, and can at most explain why subsequent records need to distinguish observation from interpretation.

v1 did not state how long the impact lasted, nor whether the compatibility window was normal. It only recorded a few terms from the incident: image resolver, defaulting, node reconciliation, and stopping retries. Brevity does not mean there was no anomaly, only that the material preserved at the time did not yet provide enough chronological detail. This version retains blank entries to avoid passing off later T+ markers as part of the initial record.

## Version Two: From Screenshots Back to the Original Input

The change in v2 was not to reword v1 more formally, but to break the incident down into several verifiable sections. The first section retains the entry point for the deviation from the baseline and the two points in time, the second adds T+00, T+07, T+18, T+31, and the third records that recovery and root cause cannot substitute for one another. It also explicitly states that the earlier screenshot-only account lacked an account, version, or run id, and could not explain why the other path worked normally.

The historical actions for KONEC-003 classified the replay of the original input as a failure on 2 2, 2026, and processing began on 2 3. What can be confirmed here is that the replay entered the handling records, and this action cannot be used to infer the specific behavior of the image resolver or node reconciliation. KONEC-008 added the sample on 2 9; KONEC-009 confirmed on 2 10 that the two versions of the record must retain separate event timelines. They supplied the missing original input, sample, and event scope, respectively, but still did not establish the root cause.

v2 also retains a correction made during the incident: "I just mistook Person on Duty for the adoption status, the previous entry is void." This sentence changed how the status field was read. It cannot be rewritten as "the field definition has stabilized", because the correction only addresses that one misreading. The other judgment, about why node reconciliation produced different results at different times, still has no corresponding counterexample.

The v2 records show that misreading the status and entry-point differences are two adjacent but distinct issues. The former comes from how people read the fields, while the latter comes from inconsistent entry-point materials at two points in time. Attributing both to the same cause produces a seemingly coherent explanation, but cannot explain why the image parser and the old records do not match. Therefore, v2 only corrected how the fields were read, without also correcting the attribution of the entry-point changes.

The branching logic used at the time was very limited: save the original input and version when the entry point is abnormal; narrow the scope of impact when the compatibility window is normal; continue checking the corresponding entry point when the comparison reaches the version matrix; stop the current retry after the user path recovers, but keep the cause open. This branching logic did not extend to adjacent projects, nor did it treat daily reports as new original records.

## Handoff trail left after v2

KONEC-008 later recorded the reason "After reviewing the existing implementation, handed it over to the module's current maintainer". It explains why subsequent checks were no longer performed solely by the person who first saw the screenshot. It does not say that the maintainer had already found the cause, nor does it treat the handoff as evidence of the scope of impact. The postmortem retains only this meaning: someone had reviewed the existing implementation, and the entry point was therefore handed over to the current maintainer.

Work on KONEC-009 resumed on day 17 of month 2. This was long after the original v1 record, and cannot be used to rewrite the unknowns in v1. It only shows that the independent incident timeline was not deleted at the first recovery. The daily report still contains only links, while the body continues to retain its own tasks-quality-signal and timeline.

The failure classification and subsequent start of work on KONEC-003 also cannot be read as "already reproduced". The action names indicate that the record moved from a failure sample into the handling stage, but do not indicate which layer produced a different revision. The supplemental sample entries for KONEC-008 likewise only expanded the materials available for review, not automatically the scope of impact. Placing the card actions in their historical context here is meant to show when the materials appeared, not to treat status transitions as technical evidence.

The handoff records also changed the entry point for review. The people involved early on started with screenshots and old records, and later the module's current maintainer, who had reviewed the existing implementation, took over. This change explains why the maintenance path shifted, but does not provide a complete link from the implementation to the revision differences. If all that remains later is the single statement "Handed over", readers will still need to return to the original input and entry-point version.

## Scope of impact

The confirmed impact is concentrated in the tasks quality signal dashboard's own entry-point records. One object reported different current revision values at two points in time, making it impossible to directly stratify failing samples for regression using the same record, and requiring attribution of unstable signals to start by determining which version was obtained. The compatibility window was still operating normally at T+07, indicating that the anomaly did not make all adjacent paths unavailable at the same time; it does not prove that all objects outside the failing samples were operating normally.

The user path recovered at T+31. Recovery here is an operational outcome: the entry point was available again, and the current retries could stop. There is no evidence establishing that the revision differences before and after recovery have been explained, nor that a particular node or the contents of a particular image must have been the trigger. Therefore, "recovered" and "explained" have remained separate throughout this page.

The scope of impact has not been extended to kubeone-compat, addons, apis, yamled, or hack. They are adjacent projects in the workspace, but this page has no corresponding original inputs, version comparisons, or event records for them. The quality signal dashboard's own failing samples can remain here; if adjacent projects show the same symptoms, they should use their own entry points and event evidence rather than copy a similar status from this page.

The impact has not been described as "all regressions have lost their baseline" either. The compatibility window at T+07 was still operating normally, which at least indicates that some paths did not show the same deviation. On the other hand, a single normal window cannot represent all failing samples, because neither how the samples entered the stratification process nor which branches that window covered was fully detailed in the original record. This narrow boundary is retained here, without turning a normal result into a global conclusion.

## Several assessments at the time

The leading assessment early on was that the defaulting path could recover. It came from the observed recovery, not from a successful comparison. This assessment was useful during the incident because it told the on-call team that they could first stop retrying, preserve the versions, and monitor the recovery page; it was not sufficient to explain what happened between the two points in time.

The second assessment focused on node reconciliation. Node reconciliation did appear in the troubleshooting context at the time, but no original snippets were retained that could connect it to the two revisions. It can only remain an unconfirmed branch of the investigation. Writing it up as the root cause would apply an unfinished working hypothesis to all the v1 and v2 material.

There were also different leads pointing to the scenario generator, embedded manifests, prechecks, and the regression entry point. In the old records, these terms were directions for investigation, not confirmed locations of changes. v3 limits them to the level of "entry points or objects to be checked", no longer making each term serve as an explanation of a cause. A lead without a corresponding file excerpt remains just a lead.

Another change that can already be confirmed concerns a misread field. Reading the on-call person as the adoption status would make the same object appear to have two official statuses; after the correction, all that can be confirmed is that this one interpretation is invalid. It does not automatically explain why the entry point reported different revision values at two points in time. The correction to the field's semantics and the change in the entry-point content need to be traced separately.

"Release freeze" was also once presented as something close to a cause. It can describe the scope that investigators at the time considered worth examining, but it cannot prove that the freeze changed the entry-point content. Similarly, the "resource task graph" and "version matrix" can help organize the materials, but no original excerpts prove that there was a fixed order between them. The old records retained these terms because they actually appeared during the search process; this postmortem does not invent relationships between them.

## What Was Saved

The original input is a tasks-quality-signal replay, rather than a reconstruction of a similar input. This restriction comes from the records in KONEC-003 and also matches the actual gap in this incident: a regenerated sample can only show the generated result, not replace the input from when the first deviation occurred.

The entry-point version and the recovery page are retained separately. The entry-point version is used to review the differences between T+00 and T+18, while the recovery page is used to confirm that the user path had been restored after T+31. Neither artifact may overwrite the other. If only the recovery page is retained, readers will not see the differences between the two points in time; if only the entry-point version is retained, there is no way to confirm that the recovery action actually took place.

The handoff record was updated to include the person handing it off, the person taking over, and the confirmation time. The historical traces in KONEC-008 show that the entry point was later handed over to the current module maintainer, who had reviewed the existing implementation. Names, statuses, and the handoff action are not treated as causes of the failure here, because this page can prove that the maintenance entry point changed, not that the object revision changed as a result.

The daily report contains only links. The scope confirmation in KONEC-009 kept this incident on its own separate timeline. The daily report can help with navigation, but it cannot replace the timestamps, inputs, and unconfirmed causes in the original records. If the daily report later retains only the line "Recovered", readers must still return to this page to see the difference between recovery and causal attribution.

There is another practical reason to retain the originals: the old records and the recovery page were generated at different times. Merging them into a single "final state" would lose the timing relationships of the anomaly, making it impossible to determine whether the deviation at T+00 preceded the recovery at T+31. Only by keeping them side by side can readers distinguish "what was observed" from "whether the flow could continue afterward".

## A Diagram of the Incident Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Original input replay] --> B[Entry-point version record]
    B --> C{Comparison of T+00 to T+18}
    C --> D[Version matrix]
    C --> E[Unconfirmed causes]
    B --> F[Recovery page]
    F --> G[T+31 user path recovery]
    A --> H[Separate incident timeline]
```

The arrows in the diagram only indicate how the materials saved on this page are consulted, not that any node has been proven to have changed the current revision. The original input replay and the entry-point version are placed on the same side, because they are used to review the deviation; the recovery page connects separately to T+31, because it only contains observations of the later recovery. The version matrix and unconfirmed causes both branch off from the comparison, indicating that they are directions for follow-up investigation and open items, not the same original record.

The separate incident timeline branches off beside the original input. The scope confirmation for KONEC-009 requires it to retain its own tasks-quality-signal and timeline, with only links in the daily report. This avoids treating another incident's summary as supplementary evidence for this incident, and also preserves the independence of the two versions of the record.

## Stopping conditions and outstanding items

When the entry point becomes available again, stop the current retry; when the comparison can only point to the version matrix and cannot provide an original snippet, do not treat matrix values as the trigger source; when the compatibility window is observed to still be functioning normally, only narrow the scope of impact, without declaring other paths unaffected; when a correction only covers how a field is interpreted, only correct the field interpretation, without also revising the node reconciliation assessment.

These were the stopping points actually used at the time, not a checklist to apply to every release incident. They arose from the gaps in this incident's records: retries do not add context to the first input, recovery to green does not automatically establish a root cause, a normally functioning window cannot cover unobserved branches, and a field correction cannot cover entry-point differences either.

Three groups of outstanding items remain. The first concerns the specific changes between time points: which object first produced a new current revision is not yet confirmed. The second concerns the relationships along the chain: no ordering among defaulting, the image resolver, node reconciliation, and the scenario generator is supported by original records. The third concerns coverage: whether samples in which the compatibility window functioned normally can represent all regression samples is not yet confirmed.

An original comparison containing the account, version, request context, and run id together is still missing. The earlier description based on screenshots does not contain these fields, so it cannot explain why the other path functioned normally. If only a single line of results is obtained later, that will still be insufficient to close these three groups of issues; it needs to be viewed side by side with the entry-point version at the time, the original input, or the recovery page.

Outstanding items still include the boundary of the phrase "two states" itself. It is suitable for describing observations at two points in time, but not for treating the object as already having two parallel formal states. The correction for the field misreading associated with KONEC-009 has retracted the interpretation "the on-duty person equals the adopted state", but it has not established a new state definition for the entry-point revision. Accordingly, whenever this page continues to use this phrase, it refers to an on-site observation, not to a model.

It is still unknown whether defaulting affects only the recovery path or also changes the content read at the entry point; it is unknown whether node reconciliation played a role in the change between the two points in time; and it is also unknown whether a stable order among the scenario generator, precheck, embedded checklist and regression entry point can be derived from the source materials. The old records successively pushed these objects to the front, and v3 put them back in the unconfirmed branch.

## Old Record Appendix

Below, several sentences that were not deleted from v1 are retained, to be understood in the original temporal context rather than elevated to current conclusions:

- "The mirror parser differs from the old records. " This was the first observation, and the source of the change was not specified.
- "Defaulting can restore it, but why node reconciliation changed is still unknown. " The first half is a working hypothesis about the direction of recovery, and the second half is a question that remains unanswered.
- "Missing time point: ____. " v1's blank entry was not later filled with a fabricated date.

v1 did not document a compatibility window, version matrix or independent incident timeline. It was only in v2 that T+00, T+07, T+18, T+31 were added, and recovery was separated from root cause. The gap is retained here so that readers can see that these contents came from later materials, rather than the early records having been reorganized into a complete timeline.

The "version matrix" "precheck" "embedded checklist" "resource task graph" and "regression entry point" added after v2 are also retained only as lookup directions in the supplementary notes where each appears. They were not merged into a unified object graph. Repeated references on the old pages indicate that the records had been stacked at the time, but that does not justify inventing new call relationships.

The sentence "I just mistook the on-duty person for the adopted state, so the previous entry is void. " in KONEC-009 is also retained as a correction made at the original incident scene. It is not a redefinition of all fields, but covers only that specific interpretation. If it were deleted, later readers could easily misread "the same object appearing in two states" as a stable state design rather than an observation during the incident.

The handoff rationale in KONEC-008 is also retained alongside the appendix. It indicates that someone reviewed the existing implementation, after which the entry point was handed to the current module maintainer; it provides no implementation snippet and does not answer who changed the revision first. The handoff, sample addendum and scope confirmation belong to different materials respectively, and cannot be combined into a single technical action simply because they all appear in the incident timeline.

This appendix remains because it shows how understanding changed: first, differences were noticed, then recovery was separated from the cause; next, problems were also found with how the fields had been interpreted; finally, the relationship between node reconciliation and the entry point version still had to be left unconfirmed. Deleting the earlier assessments would give the impression that the boundaries of this incident timeline were known from the start, which does not match the artifacts actually left behind.

## Scope of the material available at handoff

Someone taking over later can start with the original input replay, look at the entry point version alongside it, and then place the recovery page at T+31. To view the separate incident timeline, follow the links back to KONEC-009; to view the added sample records and original input processing, go back to KONEC-008 and KONEC-003, respectively. Keeping these separate here is not a formatting convention, but a way to prevent one card's later state from overwriting another piece of incident evidence.

What can be confirmed from this page is: tasks' own entry point showed different current revision values at two points in time; the image resolver did not match the older records; the compatibility window was still operating normally at relative time T+07; the user path recovered at T+31; the misinterpretation of the fields was later explicitly retracted; the original input, version, recovery page, and separate incident timeline were all preserved. These form the visible part of the incident record.

What cannot be confirmed from this page is: which object changed first; the actual order of defaulting, node reconciliation, the image resolver, the scenario generator, preflight checks, the embedded manifest, and the regression entry point; how many failing samples the compatibility window can represent; and whether the recovery action changed the current revision. These points have appeared in different follow-up notes, but having appeared does not mean they have been shown to corroborate one another.

If you only see the recovery page, it is easy to conclude that "the problem is over"; if you only see v1, you will miss the field misinterpretation and the confirmation of the separate incident timeline's scope. v3 puts these materials back in place in the order they appeared, preserving both the earlier assessments and the later changes of position. It is still a stale incident record page, usable as a starting point for investigation but not as a finalized explanation of the cause.

## Questions left in the margins at the end

Why did the same entry point show different current revision values at two points in time? There are not currently enough original artifacts to answer that. Did defaulting affect only the recovery path? The comparison has not been completed. Was node reconciliation involved in the change? There is no corresponding snippet. Is there a reproducible order among the scenario generator, preflight checks, and the embedded manifest? This has not been confirmed on this page. Which regression samples can the compatibility window's normal results cover? There is no conclusion on that either.

It has not yet been confirmed whether the content read by the entry point before and after recovery came from the same version artifact, nor whether "the image resolver differs from the old records" was actually due to a difference in inputs, a difference in resolution, or the time gap between the two records themselves. These possibilities are not arranged into a new list of root causes here, because the existing artifacts can only establish that they were avenues that had been examined.

This page therefore remains a citable but partly outdated incident record. It can help readers find the original input, the entry-point version, the recovery page, and the separate incident timeline, and can also help avoid mistaking the person on duty for the adoption status; it cannot replace a reproduction with context, much less recast the restoration of the user path as meaning that the root cause has already been confirmed.

Use this checklist only before the window closes. First open the current entry point from `docs/adj-yamled/release/yamled-dependency-boundary-audit-short-checklist-before-window-close.md`; do not substitute another page with the same name. # Decision Record: Dependency Boundary Cache Trade-offs

The audit of yamled-supply-boundary is paused at the current revision. The issue here is not to bring in both the cache and the original environment, but to decide what to retain for this assessment: keep tracing node reconciliation, or split out the release freeze.

The decision is to retain the current revision without rebuilding the environment first; the release freeze will be assessed separately, no longer treated as a status attached to node reconciliation. This is not because rebuilding the environment has no value, but because the existing records already separate the failure exits for the two paths. Collapsing them into one exit now would leave later exit actions without a clear target.

Two approaches were compared. The first was to continue tracing node reconciliation, treating the cache and the environment as part of the same problem chain. This has the advantage of fewer entry points, but the two failure exits recorded in `docs/adj-yamled/decisions/yamled-supply-boundary-cache-vs-original-state-tradeoffs.md` are not the same; merging them would make it impossible to specify which part should stop. The second was to rebuild the environment first, then take fresh samples from a clean state. That approach is deferred; the material available is not sufficient to make rebuilding a prerequisite.

Retaining the current revision does not mean treating the cache as a substitute for the original environment. The cache can only show what was on hand at this handoff; the original environment remains a separate matter. The objection is precisely that conflating the two in the record could lead readers to mistake the existing cache for a reproduced environment. That concern is valid, so the record retains the status "not rebuilt" rather than changing it to "confirmed."

With the release freeze split out, the node reconciliation assessment covers only that path; freeze-related exit actions will be listed separately later. This at least avoids restoring both paths together on withdrawal. We have not yet established which callers are using it, and the rollback boundary has not been defined. In particular, we cannot settle in advance here whether withdrawal restores only the old entry point.

This choice is narrow in scope: it only governs how the current revision is retained and how the two assessments are recorded separately. It does not claim that we already have the complete original environment, nor does it set the order of future exit actions. If results from the exit actions are obtained later, they should be appended to this record, preserving the choice made here and the questions that were open at the time.

# Public Entry Point Maintenance Discrepancy Review

This discrepancy occurred during a maintenance window for the team's public entry point. The visible result expected under the original plan did not appear. The team initially treated it as an entry point anomaly rather than immediately attributing it to a particular maintenance step. After temporary recovery, the entry point could still be used to close out the window. At the time, there was not enough evidence to establish where the discrepancy began or to determine whether similar entry points were affected at the same time.

## Records from the Window

At the start of the window, maintenance was still proceeding according to the original plan. The team retained an image resolution matrix to compare the expected results with what the entry point actually displayed. The matrix served only to preserve the basis for the comparison made during that shift: it could show that the plan and results did not match, but could not establish where the discrepancy began on its own.

After the discrepancy was first discovered, the record distinguished two things: the discrepancy already visible at the entry point, and the temporary recovery needed to let maintenance continue. This distinction mattered at the time because the recovery action had a clear target, while the cause assessment did not. No evidence was found that was sufficient to pin the issue on image resolution, the window plan, or a particular part of entry point maintenance.

The response prioritized restoring the public entry point. After recovery, the visible result returned to a usable state, allowing the maintenance window to proceed to completion. The "recovered" status recorded here describes only the action completed at the time; it does not mean the discrepancy had been fully explained or that every item in the image resolution matrix had been checked again. These two meanings can easily become conflated in a later review.

Before the window ended, no verifiable record of the actual impact scope had been produced. What could be retained was that a visible discrepancy had occurred during a specific maintenance operation and that the team had applied a temporary fix in response. Unrecorded details included which consumers had seen the anomaly, how long the discrepancy lasted, and whether it was limited to this public entry point. These gaps should not be filled in later based on impressions of the recovery result.

## Additions During the Review

The review added three control points: record the actual impact separately, make the coordinator identifiable from the window record, and retain the old entry point from before temporary recovery in a rollback-ready state. Keeping the old entry point does not make it a long-term alternative. It prevents recovery from leaving only one result available for inspection, with no way to return to the original entry point and check the differences observed during the shift.

If the same situation occurs again, first record the correspondence between the window plan, the actual entry point results, and the image resolution matrix, then perform recovery. After recovery, "the entry point is usable" and "the cause of the discrepancy is confirmed" should still be recorded separately. The former is a result that occurred in this instance; the latter was not established during this window.

This record preserves the operational view at the time. It can help explain why the old entry point was retained and why the recovery time was not treated as a root-cause finding, but it cannot fill in the impact scope that was not recorded during the shift or replace any maintenance notes that may be produced later.

# Common Questions About Public Entry Point Maintenance

This FAQ preserves the old guidance from the R29 release closeout period. It was originally used to answer the three questions that kept recurring on the release card, and in doing so compressed several different judgments into shorthand: the entry point had run, withdrawal of the candidate path, and addon rendering differences. The latter two were not recorded separately at the time; the page remains here so people can understand why someone later used the wrong entry point, not as the procedure in use.

**What can the existing release-e2e entry point prove?**

It can only show that the regression entry point ran on that commit and left an entry-point result. The initial draft treated "running to completion" as evidence that there was no new blocker on the release side; that was a working judgment at the time, and only later field feedback separated it from release closeout. The team's wording is: the release card may be closed only when the three cumulative chains—public behavior, the regression entry point, and rendered artifacts—are closed on the same commit, and a non-implementer has reviewed the failure boundary. The failure boundary here is not rerunning the success path; it is the difference in which a single passing run cannot hide a known failure.

This wording also does not mean checking off the three items in parallel. The old record only required them all to point to the same commit; it did not substitute the entry-point result for the rendered artifacts or the rendering result for public behavior. The initial draft did not spell out this distinction. FAQ also did not list what records each of the three chains should have attached, so the passing result of release-e2e cannot be used to infer that the rendered artifacts are complete, much less to complete the review in place of a non-implementer.

**Who is responsible for withdrawing the candidate path?**

This page does not assign specific ownership. The old answer phrased the question as "withdraw it when the candidate path can no longer be maintained," without distinguishing who proposes the withdrawal, who checks the regression results, or who accepts that decision on the release card. DOC-50 can preserve the result of a single-variable rerun; it does not record who accepts the withdrawal. As a result, someone once pressed for a withdrawal based directly on this page, but could only go back to the candidate-path records for clues. This gap is not filled in on this page; the rerun record cannot be treated as a determination of responsibility.

**Can it be closed when the addon rendering difference is missing?**

This page cannot answer that. The question can be logged, but at the time there was no corresponding rendered artifact, and it was not stated whether the difference affected public behavior. The old FAQ once conflated it with a general entry-point failure, as if a passing entry point meant there was no need to ask further; that was an extension of the old judgment above. Later, all that remains here is unknown: it is neither sufficient on its own to let the release proceed nor enough to block the release card based solely on the question's name. When a decision is needed, first check whether there is already an artifact and a corresponding public-behavior record for the difference; if not, it remains at the logging stage.

The recheck did not overturn the first run; it narrowed the original interpretation. We still held the repository state at release-e2e, the call entry point, and the base/gold node results fixed, varying only one input condition. The first visible divergence in the first run was recorded at the time as a signal of an entry point difference. After checking along the old entry point this time, we can no longer treat it as a cause. It only shows that the input in this run was not masked by the other fixed conditions.

The old entry point was marked as eligible for withdrawal in the log to identify the affected entry point during coordination, not to indicate that a decision to withdraw it had been made. The actual impact was not filled in during this recheck, and the coordinator has not provided a summary either. There was no third run, so the first two runs are not combined into a final result.

This page still stops at the first divergence. The order of the two original runs has not been rewritten: first inspect the nodes with the state and entry point fixed, then vary the condition on its own. The recheck only corrected the interpretation of the divergence; it added no new node results. Reading it as confirmation that the old entry point had already become invalid would go beyond what was recorded at the time.

If reruns continue, vary only that same input condition. If the repository state, call entry point, and node results are all changed together, the divergence is no longer comparable. DOC-51 record this round's decision and reservations. This page preserves the rerun observations; it does not decide whether to keep or withdraw the old entry point, nor does it recast the old assessment as a new operational conclusion.

The coordinator still needs to fill in the actual impact. The old entry point is only marked as eligible for withdrawal; whether to withdraw it remains undecided. The node results remain in the original log as the fixed part of both runs.

# Shared Entry Point Maintenance Decision Record

In the team's shared entry point maintenance review, Prism Cloud Infrastructure considered only two options: retain the existing `release-e2e` entry point, or adjust the release window first and then address the entry point.

The decision was to retain `release-e2e` as the current shared entry point; the window may be adjusted based on the coverage already in place, but adjusting the window must not be interpreted as replacing the entry point.

The basis for the decision is not evaluated file by file or explanation by explanation. The frozen repository's actual entry point, version matrix, and reproducible live test must all line up at the same time; only then can this portion of release compatibility be considered substantiated. Compatibility here is a cross-module contract, not a matter of listing all the involved files.

Do not delete the old entry point yet; keep it as a reversible path. The integration lead owns coordination and will follow up with callers for confirmation; `DOC-01` retains a local recheck record for the init call relationship. Matrix combinations not yet covered are not approved as part of this decision.

versions.body:
# Public Entry Point Maintenance Decision Record

The starting point for this discussion was not to rename `release-e2e`, but that the public entry point for Prism Cloud Infrastructure's team now handles releases, compatibility checks, and integration testing with callers. The entry point itself appears stable, but discussions about the window tend to conflate three things: which versions remain within the release scope, which scenarios have actually been verified, and whether callers need to change how they enter.

This record therefore treats the entry point and the window separately. The entry point is a collaboration boundary; the window is that boundary's scope of applicability over a particular part of the version matrix. The two are related, but the former does not automatically establish the latter, and adjusting the latter must not, by itself, require callers to migrate.

The initial draft recorded only the conclusion to "retain the entry point and revisit the window." During verification, we cross-checked the actual entry points in the frozen repository, the version matrix, and reproducible test results, and added a constraint that had not been stated clearly at the time: release compatibility is not a property of a directory, an e2e file, or the result of a single run. It depends on cross-module combinations still being verifiable through the same entry point. `test/e2e/scenario_upgrade.go` was one of the locations inspected while tracing back from call names, but it cannot be the sole basis for determining ownership of the public entry point.

## This Decision

Retain the current `release-e2e` entry point rather than replacing it on the grounds of "adjusting the window first." Window adjustments apply only within the portion of the version matrix covered by existing evidence; combinations outside that scope remain unchanged, and conclusions about neighboring combinations cannot be applied to them.

This decision has three direct consequences.

- Callers continue to use the existing public entry point and do not need to switch paths immediately because of this review.
- Changes to the version window must be tied to the verified scope of the matrix. Any scope without reproducible test results must be described as neither supported nor excluded.
- The old entry point is retained as a rollback path. If cross-module inconsistencies appear within the adjusted window, we can return to that entry point to continue diagnosis, rather than deleting it first and then asking everyone to piece their workflows back together.

Retaining the entry point is not a promise that it will never change. It simply removes entry point replacement from this round of window discussions and defers the decision until there are separate caller-impact and verification materials for the replacement itself. This avoids a common misreading: interpreting a narrower release window as meaning that the public entry point is no longer valid, and then making unnecessary changes on the caller side.

## The Two Approaches Compared During Review

### Continue Using the Existing Entry Point

The first approach is to retain `release-e2e` and focus the work on the version matrix and actual test coverage. Its benefit is not "changing nothing," but preserving an entry point that everyone already knows how to find: when version compatibility is disputed, release work and integration testing still begin their checks from the same entry point.

The cost of this approach is also clear. As long as the entry point remains, people can easily mistake its availability for the availability of the entire matrix; the entry point must therefore be accompanied by a clear distinction between verified windows and windows that are not yet confirmed. The entry point provides only a shared starting point, not a substitute for assessing the matrix.

### Adjust the Window First, Then Address the Entry Point

The second approach is to make the window the only initial change, then consider whether the public entry point should change along with it. The review did not adopt the approach of proceeding directly from this to an entry point adjustment. The reason was not that the window could not change, but that the available material supported assessments of only part of the window and could prove neither that all callers had moved away from the old entry point nor that the replacement retained the same cross-module verification capabilities.

Changing the entry point first would turn the question from "which versions have been verified" into "where each caller has gone." This would add coordination work without filling the gap between the version matrix and actual testing. For release compatibility, a path change cannot replace actual testing.

## Impact Record

The actual impact of this decision is limited to how the public entry point is maintained and how covered windows are described. Existing callers are not required to change entry points; the description of verified scope can be adjusted according to the matrix; unverified scope remains unconfirmed. No material supports extending the window changes into a blanket release policy, and none supports generalizing a passing result in a single scenario to the entire compatibility window.

The impact on coordination is more specific. The integration lead is responsible for collecting caller feedback on retaining the entry point and changing the window, and bringing that feedback into the same round of assessment, rather than letting each caller interpret version compatibility independently. When disagreements arise, first determine whether they concern the entry point, the version matrix, or reproducible testing; these three types of issue require different supporting materials.

- If the dispute is about whether the entry point is still being called, the coordinator first confirms the callers' entry points, rather than treating version results as evidence of call relationships.
- If the dispute is about whether a version remains within the window, first return to the version matrix and confirm whether that combination falls within the scope covered in this round.
- If the dispute is about the compatibility of a combination within the window, reproducible test results must be obtained. A single verbal confirmation, screenshot, or old link can help pinpoint the issue, but cannot independently expand the approved scope.

`DOC-01` can be used to trace init call relationships. It provides local pointers for inspection; this decision does not elevate it into a comprehensive description of the release entry point or use it to infer the behavior of callers that are not listed.

## Coordination and the Old Entry Point

The integration lead serves as the point of contact for coordination. This arrangement does not centralize all judgments in one person, but prevents release work, the version matrix, and caller changes from producing disconnected conclusions. When the window needs adjustment, the coordinator should first bring the proposed scope and existing test results together, then confirm whether any callers still depend on `release-e2e`; only when both sides are clear can the window change be communicated externally.

Limits have also been placed on how the old entry point is retained. It remains as a rollback point, not an alternative route for bypassing matrix verification. If the adjusted window exposes cross-module differences during integration testing, we can roll back to the old entry point to continue comparisons; rolling back does not automatically restore all windows, nor should it be interpreted as approval of previously unconfirmed combinations.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[release-e2e Public entry point] --> B[Version matrix]
  B --> C[Reproducible test results]
  C --> D[Covered window]
  D --> E[Caller coordination]
  E -->|Cross-module differences arise| A
```

The loop in the diagram shows the purpose of retaining the old entry point: it brings disputes back to a shared starting point for verification, rather than conflating entry point changes, matrix assessments, and test results into a single conclusion.

## Dissenting Views Retained

During the review, some favored completing the window adjustment and entry point replacement together, arguing that retaining the public entry point over the long term would make the boundary seem insufficiently clear. This concern is valid: the entry point's name alone does not tell readers which versions have been verified. However, the current material addresses window coverage, not the full impact of the replacement entry point. Bundling the two tasks would present still-unconfirmed matters as a completed migration.

Another view was to maintain only the version matrix and no longer include the public entry point in coordination. This approach was not adopted. The version matrix can explain the scope of applicability, but it cannot replace the shared entry point used by callers; when issues arise between modules, the lack of a common entry point would push reproduction and comparison into separate local workflows. This decision retains the entry point precisely so that the matrix and actual testing can still return to the same verification path.

These dissenting views have not been removed because they define the conditions for reopening the discussion: if the caller impact of replacing the entry point is clear, and the replacement can still maintain the correspondence between the actual entry point, the version matrix, and reproducible test results, entry point changes can be addressed in a separate decision. At that point, this round's decision to "not replace it for now" should not be treated as a long-term prohibition.

## Current Boundaries

Only the scope covered by existing evidence is approved in this round. Any version combination outside that scope still requires separate matrix evidence and reproducible test results. The scope must not be expanded on the grounds that the public entry point remains in place, that rollback to the old entry point is still possible, or that a neighboring scenario has passed.

One issue remains to be disentangled after the window adjustment: whether callers' reliance on the entry point name is limited to routine integration testing or has already extended into release scripts and other fixed workflows. The available material is insufficient to determine this. Once the coordinator has gathered information on the actual caller impact, the issue should be reassessed together with entry point replacement; until then, retaining the entry point and restricting the window is the only combination in effect for this round.

This record also retains the reminder from the initial draft: release compatibility should be treated as a cross-module contract, not a list of files. Repository paths, the version matrix, and actual test results are each necessary clues; only when they point to the same scope can that scope be described as confirmed.
